deck: Introduction to Head and Neck Cancer
text:
What is cancer?
Normally, our bodies have signals that tell
cells when to stop growing, but cancer
cells ignore these signals.

They keep multiplying and can form
lumps called tumors in different parts of
the body or they replace the healthy cells
in bone marrow and blood.

These cells can directly spread into, or
invade, surrounding tissues, spread to
lymph nodes, or spread to other organs in
the body, like the lung.

deck: Introduction to Head and Neck Cancer

What is the most common type
of head and neck cancer?
The most common type of head and neck
cancer is mucosal squamous cell
carcinoma.

This cancer begins in squamous cells,
which are tiny ﬂat cells that cover and
protect your mouth, throat, and voicebox.

It is important to know that squamous
cells also cover many other parts of you
body, like your skin and lungs. If cancer
starts from these cells, this is not
considered head and neck cancer.

head and neck cancer?
Salivary gland carcinomas are the other
major type of head and neck cancer.
These can start in any of the 3 major pairs
salivary glands, which make saliva and
release it into the mouth.

Salivary gland cancers can also start from
minor salivary glands, which line your
mouth, throat, and voicebox.

broken tooth, dentures, or constant biting of

inﬂammatory disorder which can lead to

attacks lining of the mouth, causing white
patches, redness, or sores.

Careful monitoring is recommended in those
affected.

I Can Manage Cancer

Biopsy
A biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing cancer. It involves
removing a small sample of tissue, which is then examined under a
microscope to determine whether cancer cells are present.

Types of Biopsy Techniques
 1 Direct tumor biopsy
Tissue is obtained directly from the
primary tumor, often using cup forceps or
punch biopsy.

 2 Needle biopsy of lymph nodes

If a deeper tumor or a suspicious lymph
node in the neck is detected, a ﬁne needle
aspiration or core needle biopsy can be
performed. These are often performed
with an ultrasound to ensure accuracy.

Types of Biopsy Techniques

Biopsies are important not only for
conﬁrming the presence of cancer but
also for identifying the type of cancer
and testing for human papillomavirus
(HPV), which can affect the treatment
plan.

What happens after
 diagnosis?

Cancer Staging

Once a diagnosis is made, your doctors
will need to determine:

● The size and location of the tumor
● The extent of local tissue invasion
● Whether lymph nodes are involved
● Whether the cancer has spread
 (metastasized) to other sites

This process is called staging.

Cancer Staging
The following are some commonly used
imaging tests. Each test has unique
advantages over other tests.

● Ultrasound
● CT scan
● MRI
● PET-CT

Your oncology team will choose the best
test or tests for you.

What does the cancer stage
mean?
Staging follows the TNM classiﬁcation
system:

● T (Tumor): How big is the tumor?
 Where is it?
● N (Nodes): Has it spread to lymph
 nodes?
● M (Metastasis): Has it spread to
 other parts of the body?

What does the cancer stage
mean?
Based on the TNM ﬁndings, the cancer
is then assigned an overall stage:

● Stage 1-2: Early stage - Usually
 smaller tumors, may not have
 spread.
● Stage 3-4: Advanced stage -
 Usually larger, there may be nodal
 involvement or distant metastases.

Staging is Important because
it Guides Treatment Strategy
Early stages (1-2) may only require one
type of treatment (e.g., surgery or
radiation alone).

Advanced stages (3-4) usually require
more than one type of cancer treatment
(e.g., surgery followed by radiation or
radiation with chemotherapy).

Refer to module 4 for more information
about surgery and module 9 for
radiation.

Staging is Important because
it Helps Predict Prognosis
Early-stage cancers tend to have higher
remission rates.

Advanced-stage cancers may have a
less favorable outlook, but prognosis
varies based on several factors.

Ask your oncology team about your
prognosis.

Curative Head and Neck Cancer Treatments:
Overview


 Medication

I Can Manage Cancer


Treatments Aimed at Cure
The main goal of curative treatment is to eliminate the cancer and
prevent it from coming back. Surgery and radiation are the two types of
treatment that are known to cure head and neck cancers. Depending on
the stage, location, and overall health of the patient, different
combinations of treatments may be used.

Surgery
Surgery is one of the main treatment
approaches for head and neck cancers.

It can treat cancers involving the mouth,
throat, voice box, nose or sinonasal
cavities, and saliva glands. It is rarely used
to treat cancers of the throat behind the
nose (nasopharynx).

Surgery is often the preferred treatment
option for cancers involving the mouth, or
oral cavity, and the saliva glands.

Surgery
Depending on the risk of recurrence,
patients may need radiation and/or
chemotherapy after surgery.

The risk of recurrence depends on the
features and behavior of the tumor.
Oftentimes, these are only fully
understood after the tumor is removed.

We discuss this topic in depth in Module 9,
which is titled “Postoperative Radiation
and Chemotherapy.”

Radiation
Radiation is the other major
treatment for head and neck cancers.

Like surgery, it can treat cancers
involving the front of mouth, throat,
voice box, nose or sinonasal cavities,
and saliva glands. It is not commonly
used as the ﬁrst step of treatment for
cancers involving the front of mouth,
or oral cavity, and saliva glands.

Radiation
Radiation is often preferred for
cancers involving the back of the
throat behind the mouth, or
oropharynx, the back of the throat
behind the nose, or nasopharynx,
and voice box, or larynx.

It is also commonly used for cancers
that are very large, difﬁcult to access,
or where surgery may cause
meaningful loss of function, such as
a reduced ability to speak or
swallow.

Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy is often added to increase
the effectiveness of radiation. Adding
chemotherapy is a complex decision that
depends on many factors including:
 - The tumor size and extent of local
 tumor spread
 - Lymph node involvement, the size of
 the lymph nodes, and whether tumor
 has spilled out of the lymph node into
 the surrounding tissues
 - The overall health of the patient and
 the patient’s ability to handle the side
 effects of chemotherapy

Chemotherapy
Your cancer treatment team will discuss
your case together and determine
whether you would beneﬁt from
treatment with chemotherapy.

Chemotherapy is usually delivered
weekly, or every three weeks, during
radiation.

It is important to know that chemotherapy
alone does not cure head and neck
cancer.

Medication Followed by Surgery
or Radiation
In some uncommon situations, systemic
therapy is given before surgery or
radiation. Systemic therapies include
immunotherapy, chemotherapy, and
targeted biologic therapy. This is called a
“neoadjuvant” approach to treatment.

Systemic therapy is also given after
surgery or radiation. This is called
“adjuvant” treatment.

Medication Followed by Surgery
or Radiation
Generally speaking, the goal of this
approach is to shrink the tumor before
surgery or radiation. Shrinking the tumor
may make it easier to completely remove
or treat.

Medication Followed by Surgery
or Radiation
Most commonly, these medications are
given intravenously, or into the blood
through needles in the veins, every 1-3
weeks.

The length of treatment with medications
before surgery or radiation is commonly
6-12 weeks, but in some scenarios, may
last many months.

Introduction to palliative cancer

Palliative Cancer Treatment: Why? I Can Manage Cancer




Sometimes head and neck cancer spreads too far or a patient’s health
prevents doctors from offering aggressive cancer treatment.
When head and neck cancer cannot be cured with surgery or
radiation, doctors may recommend palliative cancer treatment.

Palliative Cancer Treatment: Why? I Can Manage Cancer




With palliative cancer treatment, doctors focus on controlling
symptoms and improving quality of life.
It is important to know that while we don’t expect palliative treatment
to be curative, in some circumstances, it may prolong survival or
provide long-term disease control.

Palliative Cancer Treatment: What is It? I Can Manage Cancer




There are several different types of palliative cancer treatment:
 - Medication, or palliative systemic therapy
 - Palliative radiation therapy
 - Palliative surgery
 - Best supportive care
 - Hospice
Forms of palliative cancer therapy

Palliative Systemic Therapy
Palliative systemic therapy is the most
common type of palliative cancer
treatment. It involves chemotherapy,
targeted therapy, or immunotherapy.

It is used when cancers are very advanced
in the head and neck, when the cancer has
spread to other organs, or when surgery or
radiation are unlikely to be curative.

The choice of drugs and intensity depends
on the patient’s symptoms, tumor, and
overall health.

Palliative Systemic Therapy
Treatment with palliative systemic therapy
traditionally means the cancer is incurable.

However, newer treatments such as
immunotherapy can sometimes make the
cancer disappear completely, for years or
more.

Palliative Radiation Therapy
Palliative radiation aims to temporarily
shrink the cancer. It also aims to reduce
symptoms from the cancer, such as pain.

There are a number of different ways
palliative radiation can be delivered.

It is often a short course of treatment; most
commonly completed in 1-2 weeks of daily
treatment.

Palliative Surgery
Palliative surgery is a less common
treatment option for head and neck
cancers. It shares the same goals of other
palliative treatment options: to reduce
symptoms from the cancer and improve
quality of life.
Overview of supportive care

Best Supportive Care
Best supportive care aims to prevent and
address the symptoms and side effects of
head and neck cancer and improve quality of
life. Unlike palliative systemic therapy,
radiation, and surgery, best supportive care
does not directly treat the cancer.

Supportive care can include pain
management, mental health support,
nutrition, respiratory support with oxygen,
swallow and speech support.

The palliative care team can help with
symptoms.

Hospice
Hospice care also aims to treat the
symptoms and side effects of head and
neck cancer and improve quality of life.

Usually, your doctors will only recommend
hospice when you are expected to live for
a short period.

Hospice care can be given at home or in a
facility.

Surgical oncologist
A surgical oncologist is a surgeon who diagnoses and
surgically treats your cancer.

Surgical oncologists:

● Take biopsies to help diagnose cancer
● Discuss potential surgical treatments
● Explain the beneﬁts and risks of potential
 surgical treatment
● Explain to you how to prepare for surgery
● Discuss with you what to expect after surgery
● Oversee your recovery from surgery

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Medical oncologist
An oncologist is a cancer doctor that specializes in
diagnosing and treating cancer with medications
like chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted
therapy, or hormone therapy.

Medical oncologists:

● Plan and discuss with you treatment options
● Help you understand the risks and beneﬁts of
 each treatment option
● Oversee your cancer treatment
● Help manage any side effects from and after
 your treatment

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Radiation oncologist
Radiation oncologists are doctors that treat
cancer with radiation therapy.

Radiation oncologists:

● Help decide if you would beneﬁt from
 radiation therapy and if so which kind
● Explain to you your radiation therapy
 options and how it works
● Design and discuss with you your
 treatment plan
● Oversee treatment and help you to manage
 radiation therapy side effects

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Speech and language pathologist (SLP)
Speech and language pathologists help with cancer and
treatment effects on your voice, swallowing, and
communication skills.

Speech and language pathologists will meet with you
before, during, and after treatment to:

● Evaluate and treat swallowing difﬁculties
● Support communication after surgeries or treatment
 affecting the mouth and throat
● Teach you safe eating and drinking strategies
● Create a personalized plan to meet your
 communication and swallowing goals

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Dentist
Dentists are doctors who specialize in treatment
of the teeth, gums, and mouth.

Dentists:

● Detect early signs of potential oral cancer
● Manage any oral complications that come
 up during and after cancer treatment
● If necessary, can help correct any anatomical
 changes or changes in eating and speaking
 with prosthetic dentistry

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Oral maxillofacial surgeon
Oral and maxillofacial surgeons are specialists
in treating conditions that affect the mouth, jaw,
and face. They work with your medical and
dental teams to protect your ability to speak,
chew, and maintain oral health.

Oral and maxillofacial surgeons:

● Treat complications affecting the mouth,
 teeth, or jaw
● Place dental implants or preparing for
 dentures after surgery
● Support cosmetic and functional recovery
 to improve quality of life.

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Dietician
A dietician is a healthcare professional that
specializes in food and nutrition. Ask your provider
to place a referral if you would like to be contacted.

Dieticians help:

● Improve and maintain your nutritional status
 before, during, and after your cancer treatment
● Manage changes in your weight or appetite
● Help you develop an eating plan that meets
 your needs
● Answer your questions on diet and nutrition
 throughout your treatment and recovery

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Social worker
A social worker helps you and your family cope
with and manage practical and emotional
challenges that come with cancer and its
treatment.

Social workers:
 ● Connect you with support groups and
 community services
 ● Help you navigate and ﬁnd resources for
 transportation, housing and ﬁnancial
 assistance
 ● Assist with paperwork and insurance concerns
 ● Advocate for you and your family's’ needs

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Counselor or Therapist
A counselor or therapist supports your
emotional and mental wellbeing and help you
address emotional, psychological, and social
challenges. This may be your
psycho-oncologist.

Counselors or therapists:

● Provide a safe space to talk
● Help you manage stress, anxiety, and
 depression
● Support you mentally and emotionally
 through your treatment and beyond.

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Chaplain
A chaplain supports you and your loved ones’
spiritual and emotional well being--regardless of
religious background or beliefs.

Chaplains help:

● Provide emotional support during difﬁcult
 moments
● Explore questions about meaning, purpose, or
 hope
● Support your spiritual or religious practices
 through treatment and treatment decisions
● Connect you with religious or spiritual
 resources in your community

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Occupational therapist
An occupational therapist helps you stay as
independent, active, and safe as possible throughout
your treatment.

Occupational therapists:

● Offer strategies to manage physical changes
 (such as weakness, limited movement and
 fatigue)
● Help to adapt your home environment for
 comfort and safety
● Recommend tools or equipment to make
 everyday tasks easier and safer
● Support your return to work, school, or hobbies

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Physical therapist
A physical therapist helps you regain strength,
balance, and mobility during and after cancer
treatment.

Physical therapists:

● Reduce pain or stiffness during and after
 treatment
● Help with walking or movement challenges
● Teach exercises to improve strength,
 mobility, and coordination
● Teach safe ways to stay active and return to
 daily routines

deck: Introduction to Your Cancer Treatment Team
text:
Physical medicine and rehabilitation
specialist
Physical medicine and rehabilitation specialists are
doctors that manage your medical issues throughout the
treatment and the rehabilitation process. They work with
physical therapists, occupational therapists, and other
specialists to optimize recovery.

Physical medicine and rehabilitation specialists:

 ● Develop a rehabilitation plan to improve movement
 and function
 ● Manage and limit pain or discomfort from cancer
 treatment or surgery
 ● Recommend equipment to help mobility challenges

Procedure Options

What does the voice box do?

● Helps you talk
● Closes off your lungs when you swallow
● Helps guide food to your stomach
 ○ After the voice box is removed, you can
 still swallow by mouth once your
 stitches heal (usually in 7–10 days)

Treatment options
 - Surgery
 - Radiation and/or chemotherapy
 - Post-op considerations specific to larynx cancer

What are my surgical options?



 Total Transoral Laser
 Partial
 Laryngectomy Microsurgery
 Laryngectomy
 (TLM)

What is the difference between a partial and total
laryngectomy?
A partial laryngectomy is surgery to
remove part of your voice box (larynx).
This may be done to remove cancer
while trying to save your ability to
speak and swallow.

A total laryngectomy means the entire
voice box (vocal cords) is removed. This
is done when cancer involves most or
all of the larynx.

What changes after a total
laryngectomy?
In a partial laryngectomy, a temporary stoma
may be used to help with breathing while you
heal.

In a total laryngectomy, a permanent stoma is
created because the entire voice box is
removed, and this becomes your only way to
breathe. Moreover, a prosthesis is needed to
speak.

What is transoral laser
microsurgery?
 ● It is a minimally invasive surgery used to
 remove tumors from the throat or voice
 box through the mouth (no open cuts on
 the neck).
 ● A microscope is used for precise vision
 ● A laser is used to cut and remove the
 tumor
 ● Usually done under general anesthesia

When is TLM used?
TLM is used most often to treat:

● Early-stage laryngeal cancer (especially
 on the vocal cords – glottic cancer)
● Supraglottic cancer (above the vocal
 cords)
● Benign vocal cord growths (like polyps
 or papillomas)
● Sometimes used for oropharyngeal
 cancers (like base of tongue or tonsils)

You will be in the hospital

Stoma Care
It is very important that you learn to care for your

Make sure to:

● Sleep with your head elevated to prevent

Daily Stoma Care
The following should be performed at least twice a
day:
• Remove soft plastic tube for cleaning so you can see
only the stoma
• Look in the mirror and spray salt water (see recipe
later) into your stoma
• Cough into a tissue held over your stoma
• Clean your stoma with q-tips, 4x4's and/or a
washcloth
• Use a mixture of 1/2 hydrogen peroxide and 1/2
water to cleanse stitches and/or staples twice a day
until they are removed.
• Place a thin coat of Vaseline or Aquaphor around the
stoma and neck to protect and moisturize.

● Use a bedside humidiﬁer.

● A neck dissection is a surgical procedure

Basic Concepts, Deﬁnitions,
 and Background to Flaps

What is a ﬂap?
A ﬂap is a piece of tissue used to ﬁx a
wound or cover a missing area after
surgery.

A ﬂap is different from a graft because it
has its own blood supply (a graft does
not).

Blood ﬂows into the ﬂap through an artery
and out of the ﬂap through a vein to keep it
alive.

What can a ﬂap be made of?
 Soft tissue (skin, muscle, fat)

 Bone

 Both soft tissue and bone

What is a graft?
A graft is a piece of tissue used to repair
or rebuild an area, but it does not have
its own blood supply.

A skin graft is very thin (like a piece of
paper) and does not need blood vessels.
It can use oxygen and nutrients from the
tissue it is placed on.

Because it is so thin, a skin graft is
mostly used for surface repairs, not deep
wounds.

Bone or Cartilage Grafts
Sometimes bone or cartilage can
be used as a graft.

Bone or cartilage grafts are small
pieces without blood supply.
They get oxygen and nutrients
from the soft tissue around them.

Free Flap
A free ﬂap is taken from a distant body part (like
the forearm or lower leg).

Blood vessels are cut to move the ﬂap to the
needed area.

The ﬂap vessels are connected to blood vessels
in the neck (artery to artery, vein to vein).

This process is like a transplant, but since it
comes from the patient’s own body, there is no
risk of rejection and no anti-rejection medications
are needed.

Pedicled Flap
A pedicled ﬂap is taken from a nearby area (like the chest or shoulder).

The pedicled ﬂap stays attached to its original blood vessels.

Key Differences Between Free
Flaps and Pedicled Flaps
A free ﬂap gives more freedom to shape
and position the tissue.

When bone is needed a free ﬂap is
usually necessary (unless the piece of
bone is very small).

Situations When the Free
Flap is a Better Option than
the Pedicled Flap or Graft
 A skin graft may be too thin and not
 work well for deep wounds.

 Skin grafts in the mouth can cause
 scarring and limit tongue
 movement.

 Skin grafts cannot be placed directly
 on bone because bone does not
 provide enough blood supply.

Situations When the Free
Flap is a Better Option than
the Pedicled Flap or Graft

 Grafts may not heal well if the area
 has had or will have radiation
 therapy.

 A pedicled ﬂap may be too thick or
 not reach the area needing repair.

How does surgery affect eating, drinking, and breathing?

The mouth and throat are important for eating, drinking,
speaking, and breathing.

Surgery in these areas can cause swelling, which may

When can I eat by mouth?
The flap (usually skin) is stitched into place to repair the surgical
wound in the mouth. Stitches dissolve in about a month, but healing
takes 2 to 3 weeks or longer. The wound must be fully sealed to
prevent saliva from leaking into the wound. Your surgeon will decide
when it is safe for you to start eating and drinking again.

Can I swallow my own
saliva while I am healing, or
should I spit it out?
Yes, you can swallow your saliva.

It is not recommended to constantly
spit or suction it out, unless you
cannot swallow. This could cause
dehydration over time.

Why is a free flap used to repair the lower jaw?

Reconstructing the lower jaw usually requires a
free flap because these cancers need radiation
therapy after surgery to prevent the cancer from
returning.

Radiation would destroy a bone graft because
the graft does not have a blood supply, but the
free flap does have blood supply.

I Can Manage Cancer

Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction Continued
Also, a free flap is used when there is a gap in the bone bigger than about
5 cm (2 inches) because larger grafts may not survive.

The bone-containing flaps that are commonly used for jaw reconstruction
are the fibula, scapula, and a small amount from the radius/forearm flaps
(AKA osteocutaneous radial forearm free flap).

Which type of ﬂap will be used
for the mandible? The ﬁbula
ﬂap
Surgeons usually use the ﬁbula ﬂap to
rebuild the jaw. The ﬁbula is a strong
bone in the lower leg that can be
shaped to ﬁt the jaw.

We also take some soft tissue (skin, fat,
and fascia) from the leg to help with the
reconstruction.

The Fibula Flap Continued
The ﬁbula’s blood vessels are long,
which helps position the new jaw
correctly.

Another beneﬁt is that while one
surgeon removes the tumor, another
can prepare the ﬁbula ﬂap at the same
time. This can save 1 to 2 hours in
surgery.

The Scapula Flap
Another option is the scapula ﬂap (from
the shoulder blade). However, since it's on
the back, it takes more time in surgery
because surgeons can’t work on it at the
same time as tumor removal.

The scapula ﬂap is often used if the lower
leg isn’t healthy enough for a ﬁbula ﬂap.
This is because leg arteries can have more
blockage (atherosclerosis), while the
scapula’s artery is usually healthier.

The Scapula Flap Continued
Unlike the ﬁbula ﬂap, the scapula ﬂap
doesn’t need a special scan (CT
angiogram) to check blood ﬂow because
the artery for the scapula ﬂap is not vital
to any other body part.

The scapula ﬂap is also a better choice
when a lot of soft tissue is needed, as it
provides more skin and muscle than the
ﬁbula.

Is the titanium plate
safe?
Yes, the titanium plate is safe and
stays in the body permanently for
most patients.

It does not cause allergies or
reactions and cannot be rejected by
the body.

Is the titanium plate safe?
Continued
The titanium plate is not magnetic,
so it won’t set off metal detectors
and is safe for MRIs.

Occasionally, the plate can become
infected over time (rarely) and need
to be removed. Another rare
complication is when the plate
becomes loose over time, requiring
removal, or the plate breaks. These
situations are rare.

Soft Tissue Repair in the
Tongue, Cheek, or Under the
Tongue
If there is a soft tissue defect in the
tongue, cheek, or under the tongue (ﬂoor
of the mouth) some skin or muscle from
the ﬂap is sutured in place to patch the
soft tissue defect.

The sutures will all dissolve on their own.

Will I look like myself after mandible reconstruction
surgery or will I be disﬁgured?
For most patients, the changes to appearance after mandible
reconstruction are minimal. Signiﬁcant changes are rare and usually only
happen if the tumor or wound affects the external skin or soft tissue of the
face or neck. This is typically seen in very large tumors.

I Can Manage Cancer
Will I have visible scars?
Generally, this surgery is done through the inside of the mouth and an
incision on the neck. It is not usually necessary to place any scars on
the face unless the tumor is invading the skin of the face or neck (this
is not common).

I Can Manage Cancer
Will I have visible scars?
A neck incision is necessary to find blood
vessels in the neck to re-establish blood
flow to the flap. These neck incisions
heal very well and leave a faint scar that
is generally not obvious after it heals.

Usually, lymph nodes need to be
removed from the neck as part of the
cancer surgery. The same neck incision
is used for this as well.

I Can Manage Cancer
Will my face shape change?
The shape of the reconstructed mandible
is based on the shape of each individual
patient’s jaw. The titanium plate is
custom made to each patient’s anatomy.

It is not possible to make the new jaw the
exact same shape as the patient's
natural jaw, however, the changes are
usually subtle once healing is complete

Swelling of the face and neck is normal
and expected after surgery. Usually, this
swelling is the worst 3 days after the
surgery and then gradually improves
over the next several weeks to months.

Swelling may come and go at times- this
is normal.

I Can Manage Cancer

When is swelling the worst?
Sometimes patients find that swelling is worse in the morning when
they wake up – because they have been lying down all night. If this is
the case, sleep with your head elevated on extra pillows, or even in a
reclining chair if necessary. Sometimes patients notice swelling
increases throughout the day, and it is better in the morning.

When should I be worried about
swelling?
If swelling is gradually worsening over
several consecutive days, this may be a cause
for concern, especially if there is also
increased pain, redness of the neck or face, or
drainage of pus from incisions or drain tubes.

The presence of fevers and/or chills is a
warning sign as well. Talk to your surgical
team.

Is this surgery painful?

This type of facial surgery is generally
less painful than most patients expect.
There is certainly some pain, but it is
usually well controlled with pain
medicine.

There may be some pain that comes and
goes. Pain may be worse at certain times
of day and some days may be worse
than others. This is normal.

I Can Manage Cancer


When is pain concerning?
Pain is worrisome if it is continually
increasing over several days.
Especially if there is also
fevers/chills, swelling that is
gradually increasing over several
days, or any new drainage from any
incisions.

mandible reconstruction in many ways.

The bones are smaller than the mandible,
so while titanium plates are still used to
join the bone segments together, these are
smaller than the plates used for mandible
reconstruction.

Plates are still usually custom made for
each individual patient.

Fibula Flap

The Fibula Flap. How is the
ﬁbula used for reconstruction?

The ﬁbula is the smaller of the two lower
leg bones (the larger bone is the tibia).

It can be safely removed and used for
reconstruction. The central part of the
ﬁbula is removed, saving the bottom 3-4
inches by the ankle, and a similar length
by the knee.

Will this affect blood ﬂow to
my leg?
The lower leg has 3 arteries that carry blood
down to the foot. The artery called the
peroneal artery supplies the ﬁbula ﬂap.

Because the leg has 3 main arteries, and if
the other two arteries are healthy, blood
ﬂow to the foot remains normal after
surgery.

How do we make sure it’s
safe?
We will check your pulses on your foot and
order a scan called a CT Angiogram, which
examines the arteries in the legs.

We do this to make sure that it is safe to take
the peroneal vessels supplying the ﬁbula ﬂap
without hurting the circulation to the foot.

What will my leg look like
after surgery?
If no skin is needed for reconstruction,
you will have a in scar, in a straight line,
running down the outside of the calf,
from below the knee to above the
ankle.

The example on the right shows a scar
after two weeks of healing—this is not
the ﬁnal result.

What happens if skin is needed for
reconstruction?
 If skin is necessary for reconstruction, the resulting skin wound
 usually cannot be closed. This leaves a shallow, open wound, with
 exposed muscle, after the ﬂap is taken.

 To repair this, we may take a skin graft from the thigh. This skin
 graft is paper thin and is used to patch the leg wound.

 It will always look somewhat like a patch, but the color will even out
 over time, and the scars will fade and become smooth.

What are my other options
for a skin graft?
More commonly, we are now using a skin
substitute called biodegradable tissue matrix
(BTM), rather than a skin graft for ﬁbula donor
sites.

This is an artiﬁcial skin substitute that helps
the wound heal.

There is a thin plastic layer covering the BTM.
The surgeon will take this off in the clinic. If
you notice it falling off, do not be alarmed.

How does BTM work?
The BTM forms a layer of
healing tissue called
granulation tissue over the
wound bed.

Once this (granulation tissue)
has formed, the body forms
skin over the BTM naturally.

How long will this healing
process take?
This process can take several
months, depending on the size
of the defect.

This is an example of what it
may look like when it's healed.

What to expect after surgery—
drain tube
There will be a plastic surgical
drain tube placed in the wound
at the time of surgery.

This is usually removed before
you leave the hospital. Drain tube

What to expect after

 There will also be a wound VAC placed
 on the donor site (the are the skin is
 taken from) in the hospital.

 Patients rarely go home with a wound
 VAC, so you don’t need to learn to

*We have additional information on the wound VAC
elsewhere

When can I walk?
You can walk and bear weight immediately
after surgery, with assistance.

Immediately after surgery, patients have
many monitors, drains, and IV lines attached
to them-- it is easy to trip and fall.

You will need to be helped when getting
out of bed while you are in the hospital,
especially while in the ICU.

Will I have pain in my leg?
The pain from the ﬁbula ﬂap is usually
less severe than people expect.

Usually, it is more bothersome after
patients start walking more at home,
and it can linger for weeks or even
months.

How long will I have pain in
my leg?
This pain resolves with time, but
sometimes it can take months or a
year.

Usually, the pain is mild soreness and
lasts about 6 months.

It is like having a sprained ankle

Will I need physical therapy?
Physical therapy is sometimes needed, but not
always.

Generally, healthy, active people regain full
mobility more quickly than patients who have a
lower baseline level of mobility and activity prior to
surgery.

Usually, active, healthy patients can walk without
assistance (meaning without a cane or walker) in a
few weeks.

Will the surgery affect my walking?
 The ﬁbula bone functions to provide stability to the ankle, in
 addition to the many ligaments of the ankle and foot that bind the
 different bones together.

 When the ﬁbula is removed, extra stress is placed on these
 ligaments.

 Over time, the ligaments strengthen and compensate for the loss of
 the ﬁbula.

 Until this happens, there will be some discomfort and instability.

Will I have have mobility issues?
Patients who have problems with strength or
mobility pre-operatively may require weeks or
months of using a walker or cane, along with
physical therapy.

This is not usually expected, but it is a possibility
to prepare for.

It is very unusual to have any permanent
mobility problems after a ﬁbula ﬂap, but healing
can be slow.

Is leg swelling normal?
Swelling in the ﬁbula ﬂap donor leg is
quite common.

If you have any swelling in the legs
before surgery, it is very likely you will
have more severe swelling in the
donor leg after surgery.

This is usually temporary

What can I do to help
the swelling go down?

You can use an ACE wrap or
a compression stocking to
help with this.

How do I use the ACE wrap?
 Make sure to wrap the leg starting at the toes, around the
 foot, and ankle.

 The goal is to provide more compression to the foot and
 ankle than to the calf.

 Wrapping the leg without wrapping the ankle will lead to
 worsened swelling because ﬂuid will be trapped below the
 compression, in the ankle.

*We have a leg dressing guide that provides more instructions on how to
wrap the leg appropriately

Scapula (Shoulder Blade)
 Flap

Is the whole scapula
used?
When the scapula is needed for
reconstruction, it is not removed in
its entirety.

Only the edge of the bone or the tip
of the scapula is taken, leaving most
of the scapula intact.

What will the incision look
like?
The incision will run along the ﬂank,
from the axilla (under-arm) down
about 10 inches or so.

The donor site wound can usually be
closed completely, without a skin
graft.

Will my shoulder function
be affected?
 It is rare to have permanent major
 functional problems from a scapula ﬂap.

 There will certainly be some soreness and
 stiffness, which may last several months.

 If necessary, we will arrange for physical
 therapy.

How sore or stiff will I feel after?
 The degree of soreness and stiffness depends on the
 amount of tissue that is needed for the reconstruction.

 Smaller tumors and smaller ﬂaps lead to less issues
 with recovery.

 Larger surgeries can have more lasting stiffness and
 soreness.
Reconstructive Surgery and Free Flaps

Will I have drain tubes?
Two rubber drainage tubes are left
in the ﬂank at the time of surgery to
drain ﬂuid that accumulates in the
surgical wound.

Usually, one drain is removed after
about one week and the second
usually stays with the patient after drain tube
they are discharged home.

How do I take care of my drain?
 The drain needs to be emptied twice daily (or more
 depending on the amount of drainage) and the output needs
 to be recorded.

 The surgeon will want to know the daily output of the drain
 in milliliters (ML) for each 24-hour period.

 When the drain output is less than 50 ML per 24-hour
 period, it may be ready to be removed.

Will ﬂuid accumulate after
the drain tube is removed?
Occasionally, ﬂuid continues to accumulate
even after the drain is removed.

This can lead to swelling of the skin that
feels soft, like a water balloon.

When you stand up the swelling will drift
down to the lowest portion of the surgical
site.

What should I do if ﬂuid accumulates
after the drain is removed?
 This ﬂuid (called a seroma) usually needs to be drained but
 the procedure is easy and usually done in the ofﬁce.

 The skin overlying the area is usually numb from the surgery
 and the ﬂuid can be drained through a small needle inserted
 through the skin.

 Sometimes this can require several drainage procedures if the
 ﬂuid keeps reaccumulating.

How long can I wait to get the ﬂuid drained?
This is not urgent – you do not need to come in the same day for
this problem.

Waiting even a week or two will be okay

What wound care do I need
to do for the scapula ﬂap?
Aside from drain care, all you need to do is
apply petroleum jelly (Vaseline or
Aquaphor) to the incision several times a
day.

This is to keep it from scabbing or drying
out.

Forearm Flap

What is a forearm ﬂap?
The forearm ﬂap consists of skin from the inner
surface of the forearm, above the wrist.

How does the hand receive
blood after surgery?
The radial artery is the blood vessel that
supplies blood ﬂow to the forearm ﬂap,
and it is removed with the ﬂap during
surgery.

Once this is removed, the ulnar artery is
the only vessel supplying blood to the
hand.

How do we make sure its safe?
To ensure the hand will be safe and have sufﬁcient blood ﬂow
after the ﬂap is taken, we do a simple, non-invasive test during
the clinic examination.

It is extremely rare to have an injury to the hand if this test
looks good.

If there is doubt as to the safety of performing a radial
forearm ﬂap, we will choose a different type of ﬂap instead.

Is any bone taken from my arm?
Occasionally, bone is
needed from the radius
(forearm bone).

This is not typical, and
unless your surgeon has
discussed this with you
ahead of time it is
extremely unlikely.

What about if bone is taken from my
arm?
 If bone is taken from this location, the part taken doesn't go
 through the whole bone.

 A partial thickness shaving is taken from the inner surface
 (About 40-50%).

 To strengthen the area, a metal plate is placed across the
 section where part of the bone was removed and held in
 place with screws.

What is the plate made of?
The plate is made of titanium (like the
mandible plate described in the lower jaw
reconstruction section).

Click here to go to the
mandible plate slide

Titanium does not react with the body or
cause allergies.

It is not magnetic, so it is MRI compatible and
does not set off metal detectors.

Will I have hand
weakness?
This procedure does cause some
temporary weakness of the hand,
and it can take months to regain a
strong grip.

This is normal and physical therapy
can help.

Wound Healing– Forearm
 Usually, the forearm donor site cannot be closed, and it
 is necessary to skin graft the forearm.

 To help the skin graft heal, a special dressing, called a
 wound VAC, is placed over it for 6 days.

 Once this is removed, there is a light dressing over the
 skin graft that you will change daily.



*We have a separate information packet on wound care for the donor site.

What happens if part of the graft doesn’t
survive?
Occasionally, some part of the skin graft does not
survive.

This can lead to muscle or tendon exposure in the
area on the forearm where the ﬂap was taken.

Generally, these issues heal without further
surgery
 Image to the left is a
 healed forearm graft

How do I care for my forearm donor site?
We have a separate information packet on wound care for
the donor site.

How do I take care of the wound?
 Management involves preventing the wound from drying
 out—Vaseline and a dressing that covers the wound are
 critical.

 If, during your care, you experience these wound issues, you
 will be provided with speciﬁc wound care instructions.

 Again, this type of wound almost always heals on its own
 and is not a major concern.

Where is the thigh ﬂap taken from?
The ﬂap is taken from the outside of the thigh.

The thigh ﬂap is based on a blood vessel that is not critical

There is no test necessary to check this blood vessel (in
contrast to the ﬁbula ﬂap and forearm ﬂap).

Will I need a skin graft?
Sometimes small openings develop along
the incision line over the ﬁrst couple
weeks.

This can generally be treated with
dressings and wound care—it rarely
requires additional surgery.

If this happens, your surgeon will provide

How long will a drain be in my leg?

When can I get my drain

What if there is still ﬂuid

This is not urgent – you do not need to

The procedure is very minor and not

What wound care do I

What wound care do I need to do for the

 Wrap your thigh with an ACE bandage, so

Am I healthy enough to

Reconstructive surgery can be lengthy,

This certainly does place stress on the

Am I healthy enough to

Your primary medical doctor (PCP) will be
asked to provide a clearance note for you
to undergo anesthesia/surgery.

If you have other medical problems, such
as heart, lung, liver or kidney problems, a
note may be needed from additional
specialists, such as cardiologist, or
pulmonologist, if applicable.

Am I too old to have this
surgery?
Most of our patients are in their
50’s-80’s.

Age itself does not lead to complications
and the overall health and functional
status of the patient are more important
indicators of ﬁtness and risk.

Am I too old to have this
surgery?
Some patients are in their 80’s and are
quite healthy. Others may be younger
and have signiﬁcant medical problems
that make surgery riskier.

The decision as to whether anesthesia
and surgery are safe for a patient is made
by a multidisciplinary team of surgeons,

What can I do to prepare for surgery?
 I Can Manage Cancer




The most important thing leading up to surgery is to maintain
good nutrition to support wound healing and to avoid any
activities that worsen wound healing.

Good nutrition requires
protein.
Protein intake should be around 1.25-1.5 g of
protein per kilogram of bodyweight per day.

Supplementing your diet with Boost, Ensure, or
other protein supplements and vitamins is good,
especially if you have difﬁculty eating

Excessive protein intake is not healthy, so it is a
good idea to work with a dietician to assist with
nutrition.

Supplements
One regular daily multivitamin is
sufﬁcient and there is no need to
take additional supplements
unless speciﬁcally instructed to
by your doctor.

Some herbal supplements can be
harmful. Discuss any of these
with your surgeon before taking.

Diabetes
If you have diabetes, make sure you are
taking all your medications as prescribed
by your primary doctor.

Avoid excessively fatty and sugary foods.

Diabetes
Uncontrolled diabetes will
compromise your body’s ability to
heal.

● If you're not sure your medicine is
 right for you, talk to your primary

● Also discuss any changes after

use prior to surgery
It is important to stop tobacco
products (smoking, vaping, dipping,
cigars, pipes, etc.) at least three
weeks before surgery.

Smoking impairs wound healing
and increases the risk of
postoperative complications.

Alcohol and tobacco

You will be asked to come to the hospital
early in the morning. The hospital will call
you the evening before surgery to tell you

Usually, they want you to come in around
5:30 AM.

You will see the surgeons and
anesthesiologists before going back to the

Once in the operating room you will
undergo anesthesia. This takes 15-20
minutes.

Then once you are asleep, we will
prepare you for the surgery by padding
and positioning your body, inserting a

Then the surgical site will be cleaned

Surgery
By the time we start the operation, it will be

Hospital Stay I Can Manage Cancer




You will be in the hospital for about 10 days after free ﬂap surgery.

Sometimes this is longer or shorter depending on the type of surgery.

Why do I have to stay for ~10 days?
The main purpose of the length of stay is to make sure the surgical
sites are healing and that the ﬂap is healthy.

Wound healing problems often do not arise until about 1 week after
surgery.

This is the main reason patients remain in the hospital so long.

Hospital Stay - ICU
The ﬁrst 3 days will be in the ICU.

This is not because you will be sick or
unstable, but simply for close
monitoring.

After this you will go to the regular
ﬂoor.

Hospital Stay – Care
You will receive physical therapy in the
hospital. This becomes more in-depth
after you leave the ICU.

You will be helped out of bed to a chair
the ﬁrst day after surgery and your
activity will be increased from there.

You will receive teaching regarding any
wound care, tracheostomy care, feeding
tube, or drain care needs.

Rehab/Nursing Facility/
"Can I go home after the
hospital?
Most patients can go home after they
leave the hospital.

● But if a patient doesn’t have anyone
 to help them at home, we might
 arrange for them to stay at a skilled
 nursing facility until they can
 manage on their own.

Rehab/Nursing Facility/
"Can I go home after the
hospital?
Physical therapists usually decide if a
patient needs to go to a rehab center
after leaving the hospital.

● They will check on you several times
 while you're in the hospital, and if
 they think you need rehab, we will
 start making plans for your stay.

Fistula and Wound Infection
When you have surgery involving the mouth or throat, the wound is
exposed to saliva.

Even if the wounds are sutured perfectly, the body needs to take over
and heal the wound or it will eventually open again.

Wound healing is more difﬁcult in the presence of saliva, but there is
no way to keep it off of the wound.

Complications
If part of the incision opens, saliva can track into the incision and down
into the neck. This is called a ﬁstula and can cause infection.

If saliva is draining into blood vessels, it can cause them to clot or
rupture, which can damage or kill a ﬂap.

Usually, a ﬁstula does not occur until about 7-10 days after surgery.

• If it does happen, we may simply watch it closely (if it is small) or it
 may require additional procedures to clean the wound, patch the
 leak or place new drains.

Flap Clotting
A clot can form in the blood vessel feeding the ﬂap and kill the
ﬂap. While this is not the type of clot that can go to your lungs or
brain and be life threatening, it can necessitate more surgery.

Luckily, this is rare and occurs in about 1 patient out of every 100
cases.

Flap Clotting
Spontaneous ﬂap clotting is most common the ﬁrst couple days
after surgery.

After this it is rare unless there is a ﬁstula or infection around the
ﬂap vessels, so the risk increases again about a week after surgery,
when ﬁstulas and infections tend to develop.

Flap Clotting Risks
The risks may be higher if you have a condition that leads to blood
clotting.

● Make sure your surgeon knows if you have ever had a blood
 clot in your legs or lungs or if blood clots run in your family.

● Clotting disorders include Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin
 mutation, Protein C or S deﬁciency, elevated homocysteine,
 dysﬁbrinogenemia, and others. These are all rare but very
 important to know about.

Flap Checks
Flap checks are done to assess the blood
ﬂow to the ﬂap and make sure the ﬂap is
alive and healthy.

A ﬂap check involves looking at the ﬂap
skin to make sure it the appropriate
color.
• The skin should look like normal
 healthy skin.
• If it is very dark or purple or extremely
 pale, this can be an indication of a
 problem.

Flap Checks
A doppler stethoscope is also used to
assess blood ﬂow to the ﬂap. This is a
non-invasive way to listen to the
pulsation of blood through the ﬂap.

Sometimes we will need to scratch the
ﬂap with a needle to assess the blood
ﬂow to the ﬂap.

When this is done you will not feel pain
from the needle stick because the ﬂap
has no sensation as it has been detached
from all nerves.

 Follow Up

Follow-up
You will follow up in your
reconstructive surgeon’s ofﬁce 1
week after discharge, then 2-3 weeks
after the initial post-op visit, then
about 2-3 months later, followed by
another 1-3 visits every 6 months.

Visits may be more frequent if there
are any wound care issues.

Your cancer surgeon and other
doctors will have different schedules.

Medication Management
It is important to check in with your primary
doctor and any specialists, such as
cardiologist, pulmonologist, endocrinologist,
after discharge from the hospital.

Some of your routine medications may
change while you are healing and dosing
may be altered during and after the hospital
admission.

Medication Management
It is very important to re-establish care with
your normal medical doctors after
discharge.

As surgeons, we are not familiar with
management of most of these medications
and can provide minimal assistance with
questions and concerns regarding
management of blood pressure, diabetes,
neurological conditions, and other medical
problems.

Basic Concepts, Deﬁnitions,
 and Background to Flaps

What is a ﬂap?
A ﬂap is a piece of tissue used to ﬁx a
wound or cover a missing area after
surgery.

A ﬂap is different from a graft because it
has its own blood supply (a graft does
not).

Blood ﬂows into the ﬂap through an artery
and out of the ﬂap through a vein to keep it
alive.

What can a ﬂap be made of?
 Soft tissue (skin, muscle, fat)

 Bone

 Both soft tissue and bone

What is a graft?
A graft is a piece of tissue used to repair
or rebuild an area, but it does not have
its own blood supply.

A skin graft is very thin (like a piece of
paper) and does not need blood vessels.
It can use oxygen and nutrients from the
tissue it is placed on.

Because it is so thin, a skin graft is
mostly used for surface repairs, not deep
wounds.

Bone or Cartilage Grafts
Sometimes bone or cartilage can
be used as a graft.

Bone or cartilage grafts are small
pieces without blood supply.
They get oxygen and nutrients
from the soft tissue around them.

Free Flap
A free ﬂap is taken from a distant body part (like
the forearm or lower leg).

Blood vessels are cut to move the ﬂap to the
needed area.

The ﬂap vessels are connected to blood vessels
in the neck (artery to artery, vein to vein).

This process is like a transplant, but since it
comes from the patient’s own body, there is no
risk of rejection and no anti-rejection medications
are needed.

Pedicled Flap
A pedicled ﬂap is taken from a nearby area (like the chest or shoulder).

The pedicled ﬂap stays attached to its original blood vessels.

Key Differences Between Free
Flaps and Pedicled Flaps
A free ﬂap gives more freedom to shape
and position the tissue.

When bone is needed a free ﬂap is
usually necessary (unless the piece of
bone is very small).

Situations When the Free
Flap is a Better Option than
the Pedicled Flap or Graft
 A skin graft may be too thin and not
 work well for deep wounds.

 Skin grafts in the mouth can cause
 scarring and limit tongue
 movement.

 Skin grafts cannot be placed directly
 on bone because bone does not
 provide enough blood supply.

Situations When the Free
Flap is a Better Option than
the Pedicled Flap or Graft

 Grafts may not heal well if the area
 has had or will have radiation
 therapy.

 A pedicled ﬂap may be too thick or
 not reach the area needing repair.

How does surgery affect eating, drinking, and breathing?

The mouth and throat are important for eating, drinking,
speaking, and breathing.

Surgery in these areas can cause swelling, which may
make it hard to breathe, sometimes requiring a
temporary tracheostomy tube (a breathing tube in the
neck).

It can also affect the ability to swallow food and liquids,
making a feeding tube necessary during healing.

I Can Manage Cancer
When can I eat by mouth?
The flap (usually skin) is stitched into place to repair the surgical
wound in the mouth. Stitches dissolve in about a month, but healing
takes 2 to 3 weeks or longer. The wound must be fully sealed to
prevent saliva from leaking into the wound. Your surgeon will decide
when it is safe for you to start eating and drinking again.

Can I swallow my own
saliva while I am healing, or
should I spit it out?
Yes, you can swallow your saliva.

It is not recommended to constantly
spit or suction it out, unless you
cannot swallow. This could cause
dehydration over time.

Why is a free flap used to repair the lower jaw?

Reconstructing the lower jaw usually requires a
free flap because these cancers need radiation
therapy after surgery to prevent the cancer from
returning.

Radiation would destroy a bone graft because
the graft does not have a blood supply, but the
free flap does have blood supply.

I Can Manage Cancer

Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction Continued
Also, a free flap is used when there is a gap in the bone bigger than about
5 cm (2 inches) because larger grafts may not survive.

The bone-containing flaps that are commonly used for jaw reconstruction
are the fibula, scapula, and a small amount from the radius/forearm flaps
(AKA osteocutaneous radial forearm free flap).

Which type of ﬂap will be used
for the mandible? The ﬁbula
ﬂap
Surgeons usually use the ﬁbula ﬂap to
rebuild the jaw. The ﬁbula is a strong
bone in the lower leg that can be
shaped to ﬁt the jaw.

We also take some soft tissue (skin, fat,
and fascia) from the leg to help with the
reconstruction.

The Fibula Flap Continued
The ﬁbula’s blood vessels are long,
which helps position the new jaw
correctly.

Another beneﬁt is that while one
surgeon removes the tumor, another
can prepare the ﬁbula ﬂap at the same
time. This can save 1 to 2 hours in
surgery.

The Scapula Flap
Another option is the scapula ﬂap (from
the shoulder blade). However, since it's on
the back, it takes more time in surgery
because surgeons can’t work on it at the
same time as tumor removal.

The scapula ﬂap is often used if the lower
leg isn’t healthy enough for a ﬁbula ﬂap.
This is because leg arteries can have more
blockage (atherosclerosis), while the
scapula’s artery is usually healthier.

The Scapula Flap Continued
Unlike the ﬁbula ﬂap, the scapula ﬂap
doesn’t need a special scan (CT
angiogram) to check blood ﬂow because
the artery for the scapula ﬂap is not vital
to any other body part.

The scapula ﬂap is also a better choice
when a lot of soft tissue is needed, as it
provides more skin and muscle than the
ﬁbula.

Is the titanium plate
safe?
Yes, the titanium plate is safe and
stays in the body permanently for
most patients.

It does not cause allergies or

Soft Tissue Repair in the
Tongue, Cheek, or Under the
Tongue
If there is a soft tissue defect in the
tongue, cheek, or under the tongue (ﬂoor
of the mouth) some skin or muscle from
the ﬂap is sutured in place to patch the
soft tissue defect.

The sutures will all dissolve on their own.

Will I look like myself after mandible reconstruction
surgery or will I be disﬁgured?
For most patients, the changes to appearance after mandible
reconstruction are minimal. Signiﬁcant changes are rare and usually only
happen if the tumor or wound affects the external skin or soft tissue of the
face or neck. This is typically seen in very large tumors.

I Can Manage Cancer
Will I have visible scars?
Generally, this surgery is done through the inside of the mouth and an
incision on the neck. It is not usually necessary to place any scars on
the face unless the tumor is invading the skin of the face or neck (this
is not common).

I Can Manage Cancer
Will I have visible scars?
A neck incision is necessary to find blood
vessels in the neck to re-establish blood
flow to the flap. These neck incisions
heal very well and leave a faint scar that
is generally not obvious after it heals.

Usually, lymph nodes need to be
removed from the neck as part of the
cancer surgery. The same neck incision
is used for this as well.

I Can Manage Cancer
Will my face shape change?
The shape of the reconstructed mandible
is based on the shape of each individual
patient’s jaw. The titanium plate is
custom made to each patient’s anatomy.

It is not possible to make the new jaw the
exact same shape as the patient's
natural jaw, however, the changes are
usually subtle once healing is complete

Swelling of the Face and Neck
Swelling of the face and neck is normal
and expected after surgery. Usually, this
swelling is the worst 3 days after the
surgery and then gradually improves
over the next several weeks to months.

Swelling may come and go at times- this
is normal.

I Can Manage Cancer

When is swelling the worst?
Sometimes patients find that swelling is worse in the morning when
they wake up – because they have been lying down all night. If this is
the case, sleep with your head elevated on extra pillows, or even in a
reclining chair if necessary. Sometimes patients notice swelling
increases throughout the day, and it is better in the morning.

When should I be worried about
swelling?
If swelling is gradually worsening over
several consecutive days, this may be a cause
for concern, especially if there is also
increased pain, redness of the neck or face, or
drainage of pus from incisions or drain tubes.

The presence of fevers and/or chills is a
warning sign as well. Talk to your surgical
team.

Is this surgery painful?

This type of facial surgery is generally
less painful than most patients expect.
There is certainly some pain, but it is
usually well controlled with pain
medicine.

There may be some pain that comes and
goes. Pain may be worse at certain times
of day and some days may be worse
than others. This is normal.

I Can Manage Cancer


When is pain concerning?
Pain is worrisome if it is continually
increasing over several days.
Especially if there is also
fevers/chills, swelling that is
gradually increasing over several
days, or any new drainage from any
incisions.

Fibula Flap

The Fibula Flap. How is the
ﬁbula used for reconstruction?

The ﬁbula is the smaller of the two lower
leg bones (the larger bone is the tibia).

It can be safely removed and used for
reconstruction. The central part of the
ﬁbula is removed, saving the bottom 3-4
inches by the ankle, and a similar length
by the knee.

Will this affect blood ﬂow to
my leg?
The lower leg has 3 arteries that carry blood
down to the foot. The artery called the
peroneal artery supplies the ﬁbula ﬂap.

Because the leg has 3 main arteries, and if
the other two arteries are healthy, blood
ﬂow to the foot remains normal after
surgery.

How do we make sure it’s
safe?
We will check your pulses on your foot and
order a scan called a CT Angiogram, which
examines the arteries in the legs.

We do this to make sure that it is safe to take
the peroneal vessels supplying the ﬁbula ﬂap
without hurting the circulation to the foot.

What will my leg look like
after surgery?
If no skin is needed for reconstruction,
you will have a in scar, in a straight line,
running down the outside of the calf,
from below the knee to above the
ankle.

The example on the right shows a scar
after two weeks of healing—this is not
the ﬁnal result.

What happens if skin is needed for
reconstruction?
 If skin is necessary for reconstruction, the resulting skin wound
 usually cannot be closed. This leaves a shallow, open wound, with
 exposed muscle, after the ﬂap is taken.

 To repair this, we may take a skin graft from the thigh. This skin
 graft is paper thin and is used to patch the leg wound.

 It will always look somewhat like a patch, but the color will even out
 over time, and the scars will fade and become smooth.

What are my other options
for a skin graft?
More commonly, we are now using a skin
substitute called biodegradable tissue matrix
(BTM), rather than a skin graft for ﬁbula donor
sites.

This is an artiﬁcial skin substitute that helps
the wound heal.

There is a thin plastic layer covering the BTM.
The surgeon will take this off in the clinic. If
you notice it falling off, do not be alarmed.

How does BTM work?
The BTM forms a layer of
healing tissue called
granulation tissue over the
wound bed.

Once this (granulation tissue)
has formed, the body forms
skin over the BTM naturally.

How long will this healing
process take?
This process can take several
months, depending on the size
of the defect.

This is an example of what it
may look like when it's healed.

What to expect after surgery—
drain tube
There will be a plastic surgical
drain tube placed in the wound
at the time of surgery.

This is usually removed before
you leave the hospital. Drain tube

What to expect after
 surgery– wound VAC
 There will also be a wound VAC placed
 on the donor site (the are the skin is
 taken from) in the hospital.

 Patients rarely go home with a wound
 VAC, so you don’t need to learn to
 manage it.

*We have additional information on the wound VAC
elsewhere

When can I walk?
You can walk and bear weight immediately
after surgery, with assistance.

Immediately after surgery, patients have
many monitors, drains, and IV lines attached
to them-- it is easy to trip and fall.

You will need to be helped when getting
out of bed while you are in the hospital,
especially while in the ICU.

Will I have pain in my leg?
The pain from the ﬁbula ﬂap is usually
less severe than people expect.

Usually, it is more bothersome after
patients start walking more at home,
and it can linger for weeks or even
months.

How long will I have pain in
my leg?
This pain resolves with time, but
sometimes it can take months or a
year.

Usually, the pain is mild soreness and
lasts about 6 months.

It is like having a sprained ankle

Will I need physical therapy?
Physical therapy is sometimes needed, but not
always.

Generally, healthy, active people regain full
mobility more quickly than patients who have a
lower baseline level of mobility and activity prior to
surgery.

Usually, active, healthy patients can walk without
assistance (meaning without a cane or walker) in a
few weeks.

Will the surgery affect my walking?
 The ﬁbula bone functions to provide stability to the ankle, in
 addition to the many ligaments of the ankle and foot that bind the
 different bones together.

 When the ﬁbula is removed, extra stress is placed on these
 ligaments.

 Over time, the ligaments strengthen and compensate for the loss of
 the ﬁbula.

 Until this happens, there will be some discomfort and instability.

Will I have have mobility issues?
Patients who have problems with strength or
mobility pre-operatively may require weeks or
months of using a walker or cane, along with
physical therapy.

This is not usually expected, but it is a possibility
to prepare for.

It is very unusual to have any permanent
mobility problems after a ﬁbula ﬂap, but healing
can be slow.

Is leg swelling normal?
Swelling in the ﬁbula ﬂap donor leg is
quite common.

If you have any swelling in the legs
before surgery, it is very likely you will
have more severe swelling in the
donor leg after surgery.

This is usually temporary

What can I do to help
the swelling go down?

You can use an ACE wrap or
a compression stocking to
help with this.

How do I use the ACE wrap?
 Make sure to wrap the leg starting at the toes, around the
 foot, and ankle.

 The goal is to provide more compression to the foot and
 ankle than to the calf.

 Wrapping the leg without wrapping the ankle will lead to
 worsened swelling because ﬂuid will be trapped below the
 compression, in the ankle.

*We have a leg dressing guide that provides more instructions on how to
wrap the leg appropriately

Scapula (Shoulder Blade)
 Flap

Is the whole scapula
used?
When the scapula is needed for
reconstruction, it is not removed in
its entirety.

Only the edge of the bone or the tip
of the scapula is taken, leaving most
of the scapula intact.

What will the incision look
like?
The incision will run along the ﬂank,
from the axilla (under-arm) down
about 10 inches or so.

The donor site wound can usually be
closed completely, without a skin
graft.

Will my shoulder function
be affected?
 It is rare to have permanent major
 functional problems from a scapula ﬂap.

 There will certainly be some soreness and
 stiffness, which may last several months.

 If necessary, we will arrange for physical
 therapy.

How sore or stiff will I feel after?
 The degree of soreness and stiffness depends on the
 amount of tissue that is needed for the reconstruction.

 Smaller tumors and smaller ﬂaps lead to less issues
 with recovery.

 Larger surgeries can have more lasting stiffness and
 soreness.

Will I have drain tubes?
Two rubber drainage tubes are left
in the ﬂank at the time of surgery to
drain ﬂuid that accumulates in the
surgical wound.

Usually, one drain is removed after
about one week and the second
usually stays with the patient after drain tube
they are discharged home.

How do I take care of my drain?
 The drain needs to be emptied twice daily (or more
 depending on the amount of drainage) and the output needs
 to be recorded.

 The surgeon will want to know the daily output of the drain
 in milliliters (ML) for each 24-hour period.

 When the drain output is less than 50 ML per 24-hour
 period, it may be ready to be removed.

Will ﬂuid accumulate after
the drain tube is removed?
Occasionally, ﬂuid continues to accumulate
even after the drain is removed.

This can lead to swelling of the skin that
feels soft, like a water balloon.

When you stand up the swelling will drift
down to the lowest portion of the surgical
site.

What should I do if ﬂuid accumulates
after the drain is removed?
 This ﬂuid (called a seroma) usually needs to be drained but
 the procedure is easy and usually done in the ofﬁce.

 The skin overlying the area is usually numb from the surgery
 and the ﬂuid can be drained through a small needle inserted
 through the skin.

 Sometimes this can require several drainage procedures if the
 ﬂuid keeps reaccumulating.

How long can I wait to get the ﬂuid drained?
This is not urgent – you do not need to come in the same day for
this problem.

Waiting even a week or two will be okay

What wound care do I need
to do for the scapula ﬂap?
Aside from drain care, all you need to do is
apply petroleum jelly (Vaseline or
Aquaphor) to the incision several times a
day.

This is to keep it from scabbing or drying
out.

Forearm Flap

What is a forearm ﬂap?
The forearm ﬂap consists of skin from the inner
surface of the forearm, above the wrist.

How does the hand receive
blood after surgery?
The radial artery is the blood vessel that
supplies blood ﬂow to the forearm ﬂap,
and it is removed with the ﬂap during
surgery.

Once this is removed, the ulnar artery is
the only vessel supplying blood to the
hand.

How do we make sure its safe?
To ensure the hand will be safe and have sufﬁcient blood ﬂow
after the ﬂap is taken, we do a simple, non-invasive test during
the clinic examination.

It is extremely rare to have an injury to the hand if this test
looks good.

If there is doubt as to the safety of performing a radial
forearm ﬂap, we will choose a different type of ﬂap instead.

Is any bone taken from my arm?
Occasionally, bone is
needed from the radius
(forearm bone).

This is not typical, and
unless your surgeon has
discussed this with you
ahead of time it is
extremely unlikely.

What about if bone is taken from my
arm?
 If bone is taken from this location, the part taken doesn't go
 through the whole bone.

 A partial thickness shaving is taken from the inner surface
 (About 40-50%).

 To strengthen the area, a metal plate is placed across the
 section where part of the bone was removed and held in
 place with screws.

What is the plate made of?
The plate is made of titanium (like the
mandible plate described in the lower jaw
reconstruction section).

mandible plate slide

Titanium does not react with the body or
cause allergies.

It is not magnetic, so it is MRI compatible and
does not set off metal detectors.

Will I have hand
weakness?
This procedure does cause some
temporary weakness of the hand,
and it can take months to regain a
strong grip.

This is normal and physical therapy
can help.

Occasionally, some part of the skin graft does not

Generally, these issues heal without further

How do I take care of the wound?

Thigh Flap

Where is the thigh ﬂap taken from?
The ﬂap is taken from the outside of the thigh.

The thigh ﬂap is based on a blood vessel that is not critical
to the function of the leg.

There is no test necessary to check this blood vessel (in
contrast to the ﬁbula ﬂap and forearm ﬂap).

Will I need a skin graft?
Sometimes small openings develop along
the incision line over the ﬁrst couple
weeks.

This can generally be treated with
dressings and wound care—it rarely
requires additional surgery.

If this happens, your surgeon will provide
speciﬁc instructions on how to care for it.

How long will a drain be in my leg?
A drainage tube is left in the thigh at the time
of surgery. This tube is about ¼" thick and is
necessary to drain ﬂuid that accumulates in
the thigh because of surgery.

Usually, the drain stays in place for a couple
of weeks and patients go home with this leg
drain.

process.

 output of the drain in milliliters (mL) for each
 24-hour period.

When can I get my drain
removed?
When the drain output is less than 30-50
ML per 24-hour period, it may be ready
to be removed.

What if there is still ﬂuid
post-drain removal?
Occasionally, ﬂuid continues to accumulate
even after the drain is removed. This can

like a water balloon. When you stand up the

This ﬂuid (called a seroma) usually needs to

How will the ﬂuid

numb from the surgery and the ﬂuid can

inserted through the skin. Sometimes this

This is not urgent – you do not need to
come in the same day for this problem.
Waiting even a week or two will be ok.
The procedure is very minor and not
bothersome for patients.

What wound care do I
need to do for the
thigh ﬂap?
Aside from drain care, all you
need to do is apply Vaseline or
Aquaphor to the incision several
times a day to keep it from
scabbing or drying out.

 Wrap your thigh with an ACE bandage, so
