that make surgery riskier.

The decision as to whether anesthesia
and surgery are safe for a patient is made
by a multidisciplinary team of surgeons,
anesthesia personnel, and other
specialists.

What can I do to prepare for surgery?
 I Can Manage Cancer




The most important thing leading up to surgery is to maintain
good nutrition to support wound healing and to avoid any
activities that worsen wound healing.

Good nutrition requires
protein.
Protein intake should be around 1.25-1.5 g of
protein per kilogram of bodyweight per day.

Supplementing your diet with Boost, Ensure, or
other protein supplements and vitamins is good,
especially if you have difﬁculty eating
preoperatively.

Excessive protein intake is not healthy, so it is a
good idea to work with a dietician to assist with
nutrition.

Supplements
One regular daily multivitamin is
sufﬁcient and there is no need to
take additional supplements
unless speciﬁcally instructed to
by your doctor.

Some herbal supplements can be
harmful. Discuss any of these
with your surgeon before taking.

Diabetes
If you have diabetes, make sure you are
taking all your medications as prescribed
by your primary doctor.

Avoid excessively fatty and sugary foods.

Diabetes
Uncontrolled diabetes will
compromise your body’s ability to
heal.

● If you're not sure your medicine is
 right for you, talk to your primary
 doctor as soon as possible to
 make sure your diabetes is under
 control before surgery.

● Also discuss any changes after
 discharge from the hospital with
 your primary doctor.

Alcohol and tobacco
use prior to surgery
It is important to stop tobacco
products (smoking, vaping, dipping,
cigars, pipes, etc.) at least three
weeks before surgery.

Smoking impairs wound healing
and increases the risk of
postoperative complications.

Alcohol and tobacco
use prior to surgery
Heavy alcohol use can also cause
postoperative complications

If you have more than one or two drinks
per day, stopping all consumption of
alcohol “cold turkey” can lead to
withdrawal symptoms.

 • It is best to wean yourself down
 over the course of a couple
 weeks.

Alcohol and tobacco
use prior to surgery
If you are drinking daily before surgery,
please let us know.

You may require medication to help
prevent alcohol withdrawal while
you’re in the hospital.

This is critical information for
appropriate anesthesia and
postoperative medications.

Alcohol and tobacco
use prior to surgery
Sometimes it is difﬁcult for patients
to be honest with their healthcare
team regarding their use of alcohol,
tobacco, or other products.

It is important to be forthcoming
with this information so that we can
make sure you have the most
appropriate care and best outcome.

What to Expect in the
 Hospital

Day of Surgery - Arrival
You will be asked to come to the hospital
early in the morning. The hospital will call
you the evening before surgery to tell you
where to go and when to arrive.

Usually, they want you to come in around
5:30 AM.
 • This is to prepare you for
 anesthesia.

You will see the surgeons and
anesthesiologists before going back to the
operating room.

Day of Surgery – Start
of Surgery
Once in the operating room you will
undergo anesthesia. This takes 15-20
minutes.

Then once you are asleep, we will
prepare you for the surgery by padding
and positioning your body, inserting a
catheter into the bladder, and inserting
several more IV lines.

Then the surgical site will be cleaned
with antiseptics.

Day of Surgery – During
Surgery
By the time we start the operation, it will be
around 8:30.

Depending on the surgery, it may be
anywhere from 5 to 12 or more hours.

A designated family member or friend will
receive updates from a nurse in the operating
room. The surgeons will talk to family/friends
when they have completed their portions of
the procedure.

Day of Surgery – After
Surgery
After the procedure is completed, you will
be transferred to the ICU and will wake up
slowly.

You may not remember anything from the
night immediately following surgery.

You may have a tracheostomy tube and
feeding tube in place (if your surgeon
discussed this with you), as well as several
surgical drains in the neck and the area
where the ﬂap was taken.

Hospital Stay I Can Manage Cancer




You will be in the hospital for about 10 days after free ﬂap surgery.

Sometimes this is longer or shorter depending on the type of surgery.

Why do I have to stay for ~10 days?
The main purpose of the length of stay is to make sure the surgical
sites are healing and that the ﬂap is healthy.

Wound healing problems often do not arise until about 1 week after
surgery.

This is the main reason patients remain in the hospital so long.

Hospital Stay - ICU
The ﬁrst 3 days will be in the ICU.

This is not because you will be sick or
unstable, but simply for close
monitoring.

After this you will go to the regular
ﬂoor.

Hospital Stay – Care
You will receive physical therapy in the
hospital. This becomes more in-depth
after you leave the ICU.

You will be helped out of bed to a chair
the ﬁrst day after surgery and your
activity will be increased from there.

You will receive teaching regarding any
wound care, tracheostomy care, feeding
tube, or drain care needs.

Rehab/Nursing Facility/
"Can I go home after the
hospital?
Most patients can go home after they
leave the hospital.

● But if a patient doesn’t have anyone
 to help them at home, we might
 arrange for them to stay at a skilled
 nursing facility until they can
 manage on their own.

Rehab/Nursing Facility/
"Can I go home after the
hospital?
Physical therapists usually decide if a
patient needs to go to a rehab center
after leaving the hospital.

● They will check on you several times
 while you're in the hospital, and if
 they think you need rehab, we will
 start making plans for your stay.

Fistula and Wound Infection
When you have surgery involving the mouth or throat, the wound is
exposed to saliva.

Even if the wounds are sutured perfectly, the body needs to take over
and heal the wound or it will eventually open again.

Wound healing is more difﬁcult in the presence of saliva, but there is
no way to keep it off of the wound.

Complications
If part of the incision opens, saliva can track into the incision and down
into the neck. This is called a ﬁstula and can cause infection.

If saliva is draining into blood vessels, it can cause them to clot or
rupture, which can damage or kill a ﬂap.

Usually, a ﬁstula does not occur until about 7-10 days after surgery.

• If it does happen, we may simply watch it closely (if it is small) or it
 may require additional procedures to clean the wound, patch the
 leak or place new drains.

Flap Clotting
A clot can form in the blood vessel feeding the ﬂap and kill the
ﬂap. While this is not the type of clot that can go to your lungs or
brain and be life threatening, it can necessitate more surgery.

Luckily, this is rare and occurs in about 1 patient out of every 100
cases.

Flap Clotting
Spontaneous ﬂap clotting is most common the ﬁrst couple days
after surgery.

After this it is rare unless there is a ﬁstula or infection around the
ﬂap vessels, so the risk increases again about a week after surgery,
when ﬁstulas and infections tend to develop.

Flap Clotting Risks
The risks may be higher if you have a condition that leads to blood
clotting.

● Make sure your surgeon knows if you have ever had a blood
 clot in your legs or lungs or if blood clots run in your family.

● Clotting disorders include Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin
 mutation, Protein C or S deﬁciency, elevated homocysteine,
 dysﬁbrinogenemia, and others. These are all rare but very
 important to know about.

Flap Checks
Flap checks are done to assess the blood
ﬂow to the ﬂap and make sure the ﬂap is
alive and healthy.

A ﬂap check involves looking at the ﬂap
skin to make sure it the appropriate
color.
• The skin should look like normal
 healthy skin.
• If it is very dark or purple or extremely
 pale, this can be an indication of a
 problem.

Flap Checks
A doppler stethoscope is also used to
assess blood ﬂow to the ﬂap. This is a
non-invasive way to listen to the
pulsation of blood through the ﬂap.

Sometimes we will need to scratch the
ﬂap with a needle to assess the blood
ﬂow to the ﬂap.

When this is done you will not feel pain
from the needle stick because the ﬂap
has no sensation as it has been detached
from all nerves.

After the Hospital and
 Follow Up

Follow-up
You will follow up in your
reconstructive surgeon’s ofﬁce 1
week after discharge, then 2-3 weeks
after the initial post-op visit, then
about 2-3 months later, followed by
another 1-3 visits every 6 months.

Visits may be more frequent if there
are any wound care issues.

Your cancer surgeon and other
doctors will have different schedules.

Medication Management
It is important to check in with your primary
doctor and any specialists, such as
cardiologist, pulmonologist, endocrinologist,
after discharge from the hospital.

Some of your routine medications may
change while you are healing and dosing
may be altered during and after the hospital
admission.

Medication Management
It is very important to re-establish care with
your normal medical doctors after
discharge.

As surgeons, we are not familiar with
management of most of these medications
and can provide minimal assistance with
questions and concerns regarding
management of blood pressure, diabetes,
neurological conditions, and other medical
problems.

Preparing for Your Head and
Neck Surgery

Optimizing Your Health Before Surgery to Reduce
Your Likelihood of Complications

What does smoking and alcohol have
to do with head and neck cancer?
● Smoking and heavy alcohol use have a
 exponential effect on developing head and
 neck cancer. This means that the effect is
 more than adding the impact of these two
 causes together.

Quitting Smoking at Least 3 Weeks
Before Head and Neck Cancer Treatment:
 Why and How to Do it

So what should I do?
We recommend you quit smoking
immediately after your cancer diagnosis
and as many weeks as possible before the
start of cancer treatment.

Since quitting is hard, we recommend you
get as much help as possible from your
clinical team, which includes your
surgeon, other oncologists, primary care
doctor, nurse, social worker, and team
members within the tobacco treatment
program.

Why should I quit smoking
immediately after a cancer
diagnosis?

 Smoking before surgery increases the
 risk of wound healing problems and
 death around the time of surgery.

 This is because quitting smoking
 improves your body’s ability to heal
 and respond to treatment.

Why should I quit smoking immediately after a
cancer diagnosis?
 Patients who receive
 intensive smoking
 cessation treatment at
 least four weeks before
 surgery have a lower risk
 of surgical
 complications.

Why should I quit smoking
immediately after a cancer
diagnosis?
 Quitting at the time of diagnosis may
 reduce the risk of your cancer returning
 after treatment.

 Quitting also reduces your risk that a
 second cancer will develop.

 Quitting smoking reduces your risk that
 your cancer will be fatal.

So what should I do? How do I
quit smoking?
Support to Stop Smoking is Available:

● Regularly talking to an expert to help you quit
 AND taking medication is the most effective form
 of treatment. Doing both are more effective than
 doing one or the other.

● A person in expertise in helping patients quit
 smoking can help you identify triggers, develop
 coping strategies and provide emotional support.

● FDA-approved medications help address cravings
 as well as withdrawal and mood symptoms.

If you’re interested in quitting
smoking:
● Ask your doctor for a referral to the UTSW
 nicotine cessation program.

● Ask your doctor for a prescription for
 medications to help you quit.

What to Expect When Quitting
Smoking
Smoking affects several key chemicals called
neurotransmitters in the brain:

● Creating alertness
● Increasing energy
● Elevating mood

Quitting can lead to feelings of anxiety and low
mood/depression as the brain adjusts to a change in its
chemistry.

Medications can help re-balance these neurotransmitters
without the harmful side-effects of smoking.

What to Expect When Quitting
Smoking
Quitting is hard but your clinical team is
here to support you.

Even so called “failures” are successes –
there is a good chance you can quit
long-term if you are able to stay off
cigarettes for one week.

Drinking Alcohol Sparingly,
If At All

Reducing Your Alcohol Intake
If you drink heavily:

● Notify your surgeon
● Reduce your alcohol intake, ideally to
 sparingly, if at all
● This means 1-2 drinks per week or
 less

We do not know if there is a “safe”
amount of alcohol intake for head and
neck cancer survivors.

Detoxing From Alcohol
● Sometimes a surgeon may
 recommend detoxing from alcohol
 before starting treatment.

● Detoxing from alcohol can be life
 threatening and may require
 admission to the hospital.

● In the hospital, they can help your
 withdrawal symptoms with
 medications, such as benzodiazepines.

What to Expect When Quitting
Alcohol
● Alcohol acts as a depressant in the body,
 affecting heart rate, blood pressure and
 breathing.

● Alcohol also interferes with the chemicals
 that affect our mood. Drinking can make
 you feel relaxed initially but later leads to
 feeling irritable and restless. Another drink
 repeats the cycle.

Why should I decrease my
alcohol use?
Continued heavy alcohol use may lead
to:

● Lowered ability of your immune
 system to ﬁght cancer
● Delayed surgery
● Longer and more frequent
 hospitalizations
● Longer recoveries from treatment

What are the beneﬁts to
quitting alcohol?
Quitting alcohol helps your body ﬁght
cancer and reduces your risk of developing
new cancers.

Quitting alcohol also reduces the severity
of treatment side effects, such as
mucositis.

What to Expect When Quitting
Alcohol
Support to abstain from alcohol is available:

 ● We can refer you to a specialized
 psychiatrist to help quit alcohol by
 managing cravings and mood symptoms
 ● Support from the clinic social worker to
 identify triggers, alternative coping skills
 and problem-solve barriers to quit
Improving Nutrition

Dietician Orientation
If you prefer information in video format please view the short video below:

Why Do I Need Proper Nutrition?
Proper nutrition plays an important role before and
after your surgery.

Proper nutrition:

● Supports wound healing
● Strengthens your immune system
● Helps the body manage the stress of surgery

Malnutrition can increase the risk of
complications, prolonged hospital stays, and
slower recovery

How do I maintain my nutrition status?
A dietician is a healthcare professional that specializes in
food and nutrition. Ask your provider to place a referral if you
would like to be contacted or need help with any of the
following listed below.

Their goals are to help you make sure you are:
● Consuming adequate protein
● Maintaining your weight
● Staying hydrated

They can also help with:
 ● Coping with potential nutrition-related side effects
 from treatment.
 ● Tube feeding assistance. For more information, refer
 to the NG tube module.

How do I maintain my nutrition status?
Protein is essential for faster healing so it’s important to
increase your protein intake both before and after surgery.

Calories are equally important for the healing process as they
help you maintain your weight.

 ● Select foods that are both high in protein and calories to
 support recovery.

 ● Drink 2-3 protein shakes a day for at least two weeks
 prior to surgery is recommended. Shakes that are high in
 protein and calories are best. For more information on
 speciﬁc brands, refer to the Dietician Orientation video at
 the start of this module.

What are good sources of protein?
Depending on tumor size and location, soft protein
sources may be easier for you to eat before surgery.

After surgery you will likely rely on soft foods,
soups, and shakes for your protein needs.

Eggs are a good source of protein. You can
incorporate dishes like egg salad, quiche, and
custard into your diet.

What are good sources of protein?
Meat is also a good source of protein: include meats
such as chicken, pork, beef, and lamb to meet your
protein needs.

● If it is difﬁcult to chew or swallow meat, opt for
 shredded or ground meat with extra gravy, or
 choose casseroles and chicken salad for easier
 consumption.

Fish is another great soft high protein food.

What are good sources of protein?
Dairy products like greek yogurt, cottage cheese, and
milk are also high in protein.

● Choosing whole milk or chocolate milk can add
 extra calories, helping you maintain your weight.

● For added calories and protein, you can prepare
 oatmeal with milk instead of water

● Creamy or chunky soup like clam chowder,
 potato, cream of chicken, broccoli, or soups with
 beans are also a good option.

What are good sources of protein?
For vegetarian protein sources, try:

● Beans, lentils, or hummus (chickpeas)

● Tofu

● Soy milk or soy yogurt

● Nut butters

● Veggie burgers
Staying Active

Why is it important to stay active
before my surgery?
Staying active before surgery can help your body
prepare and recover more quickly.

Generally, healthy, active people regain full mobility
quicker than patients who have a lower baseline
level of mobility and activity prior to surgery.

Usually, active, healthy patients can walk without
assistance (meaning without a cane or walker) in a
few weeks.

Preparing for Your Hospitalization and
Discharge

Preparing for Your Hospitalization After
 Free Flap Surgery and Tracheostomy

Bring a Caretaker
If possible, plan to have a family member or a loved
one stay with you in the hospital for at least the ﬁrst
few days after your surgery.

It is helpful to have someone with you that knows
you well and who can anticipate your needs to
support you while you recover.

You will have your own room with a private
bathroom. There will also be a recliner or pull out
bed so your support person can stay comfortably
with you.

What else should I bring?
To help you feel more at ease during your stay, we
encourage you to bring a few comfort items and
things to keep yourself entertained, such as:

● Cozy socks or slippers
● A favorite blanket
● A sound machine or headphones
● A tablet
● Puzzles or games
● Books or magazines
● Pictures of loved ones

What else should I bring?
Most likely you will be unable to talk right after your
surgery so it is a good idea to have a way to
communicate your needs.

While a caregiver can help, you can also use the
following to help communicate:

● A whiteboard and a marker (provided by the
 hospital)
● Phone-based apps like a talk to text app or a
 notes app
What to Expect When You Wake Up

What To Expect When You Wake Up

The ﬁrst few days after surgery require the most
adjustment as you grow accustomed to your trach
and the changes with your surgery, the hospital
setting and the close monitoring of your progress.

Remember, you will adjust to these changes and
your hospital team is there to support you.

What To Expect When You Wake
Up
When you wake up, you will be coming out of a
major surgery and still feeling the effects of
anesthesia. This is completely normal.

You will be given pain medication to keep you
comfortable but it may also make you feel groggy,
sleepy, or a little confused at ﬁrst.

You will likely rely on your caregivers or written or
text-based forms of communication, at ﬁrst.

What To Expect When You Wake
Up
When you wake up from surgery, you will likely have
several thing attached to your body, such as a
tracheostomy, drains, tubes, or monitors.

● These are all in place to help you heal and will be
 removed as you recover.

It is helpful to remember that the ﬁrst few days after
surgery can be the hardest to adjust to but your team
is there to support you through this difﬁcult
experience.

Will I be able to eat and drink?
Because your surgery involves the head and
neck, you won't be able to eat or drink by
mouth when you wake up.

Your care team will ensure you receive
nutrition in other ways until your surgeon
determines that it is safe for you to resume
eating and drinking again.

How independent will I be after
surgery?
At the beginning, you will need help from the
hospital staff to do most things--this is
completely normal and expected.

You may also need to rely on your caretaker during
this time to communicate your needs.

● Having someone who knows you well can be
 comforting and can help ensure your care
 team understands your wishes.

How independent will I be after
surgery?
You will be moving around and encouraged to get
out of bed the ﬁrst few days with assistance.

During your stay, you will gradually regain strength
and be able to move around more on your own, but
this won’t happen right away.

Your care team will be there to support you every
step of the way. This team includes physical and
occupational therapy.
What to Expect in the ICU

What to Expect in the ICU
When you ﬁrst wake up from the surgery, you will be
placed in the Surgical Intensive Care Unit (SICU).

In the SICU you will have your own room with glass doors
that can be closed for privacy and to maintain a quiet
environment.

There is a lot of activity in the SICU and a lot of people
coming to check on various aspects of your healing.

 ● After your reconstruction, your team will be monitoring
 your new free ﬂap frequently to make sure your new
 tissue is healthy and healing.

What to Expect in the ICU
The ﬁrst few nights in the ICU may not
provide quality restful sleep.

It is important to ensure you have items that
will make you as comfortable as you can be.

Comfort Care in the SICU
In the SICU, your pain medication will likely be given
through a device called a Patient-Controlled
Analgesia (PCA) pump also known as a “pain button”.

● This device allows you to self-administer
 medication for pain relief by pressing a button.

If you are tall or you ﬁnd that your feet touch the
headboard, the hospital can provide a bed extender.

● You can also ask you care team ahead of time if you
 think you might need one.

Can I have visitors in the ICU?
Yes, you can have visitors in the ICU.

Check with the front desk to ﬁnd out the visitor policy.
What to Expect on the Recovery Floor

What to Expect on the Recovery Floor
After a few days, you will be transferred from the
ICU to a recovery ﬂoor.

Here you will have a private room (with a full bath)
with doors that can be closed for privacy and to
maintain a quiet environment.

There is less activity here as well.

● While your care team will still be monitoring
 your healing, it will be less frequent than in the
 ICU.

What to Expect on the Recovery Floor
On the ﬂoor, your pain medication will likely be given PRN
which means as needed.

 ● This means your pain medication will not be given at
 set times, but instead when you ask for it. This gives
 you more control over when you receive pain relief.

 ● It is important to pay attention to how you are feeling
 and let your care team when you are feeling
 uncomfortable.

Don’t wait until the pain is severe--your team is here to
help manage your pain and keep you as comfortable as
possible.
Planning for Discharge

Planning for Discharge
As you get closer to leaving the hospital, a care
coordinator will help ensure everything is in place for
a smooth and safe discharge.

They work closely with your doctors, nurses, and
caregiver to:

● Coordinate arrangements following your
 discharge including medical equipment,
 prescriptions, nutritional supplements.
● Answer any questions you have about your
 discharge plan.

Where will I discharge to?
When it's time to leave the hospital, your care team
and care coordinator will talk with you and your loved
ones to help choose the best option for your recovery.

Common discharge options include:
 ● Home with home health
 ● To a nursing facility
 ● To a rehabilitation facility

More information about each of these discharge
options will be provided on the next slides.

Where will I discharge to?
Home with home health:
 ● You go home but have a home health
 provider visit you a few times a week to
 help with things like wound care and
 medications.

Where will I discharge to?
To a rehabilitation facility:
 ● You go to a rehab center for more intensive
 therapy, like physical or occupational therapy,
 to help you recover strength and function
 before returning home.

To a skilled nursing facility:
 ● You temporarily stay at a facility where you
 can get more hands-on medical care and help
 with daily activities until you are stronger.

Planning for Discharge
Before you leave the hospital, your care team will help you schedule follow-up
appointments with your treatment team before you discharge.

 ● You will be coming back in about a week for a follow up appointment with
 your surgical oncologist and your reconstructive surgeon.

Planning for Discharge
Should you go home with any medical equipment your hospital team will provide
education on the items you will discharge with.

● This may include things like tracheostomy training, wound vac training,
 wound care training, feeding tube training.

Support at Home
If possible, after you leave the hospital, having help
from a caregiver or loved one will be very
important. Caregivers are encouraged to reach out
to the care coordinator if any questions arise.

They can assist with daily tasks, help manage
medications, and provide emotional support as you
continue to recover at home.

If you have any questions or concerns at any point,
don’t hesitate to talk with your care team—they’re
here to help and support you throughout your
recovery. Additionally, caregivers can contact the
care coordinator if they have any questions.
The Modiﬁed Barium Swallow Study

What is a Modiﬁed Barium
Swallow Study (MBS)?

A modiﬁed barium swallow study is a
video X-ray that shows how food and drink
move through your mouth and throat when
you swallow. It helps check how well your
throat muscles are working and how food
travels into the top part of your esophagus
(food pipe). It speciﬁcally tests the safety
and efﬁciency of your swallow.

What is the Process of getting
an MBS?

During testing, you will be seated in an
open x-ray machine. Video x-rays are
recorded as you swallow liquid and bites
of food.
The food and drink you consume is tinted
with barium, which allows it to be seen
under an x-ray.

What Happens if you have
Difﬁculty Swallowing?

The MBS study helps your care team ﬁgure out which foods and drinks
are safe for you to eat.

It also lets the speech pathologist see if you might beneﬁt from
swallowing therapy.

Having this test done before head and neck cancer treatment can help
your team plan for your nutrition and decide if a feeding tube may be
needed after treatment.

How Should You Prepare for the
Test?
● You can eat and drink normally before
 the test; there are no restrictions.
● Bring any food or drink you ﬁnd hard to
 swallow so we can observe you
 ingesting them.
● Avoid wearing jewelry or clothing with
 metal.
● If you use special drinking tools (like a
 straw or bottle), please bring them.

How Should You Prepare for the
Test?
● Please arrive 30 minutes early to allow
 time for check-in.
 ○ Check in at the Outpatient Building:
 1801 Inwood Rd, Dallas, TX 75390,
 1st ﬂoor.
● On MyChart, your MBS appointment will
 appear as an X-ray visit followed by a
 speech pathology visit. Both are done
 during the same visit at the outpatient
 building.
● For any questions, please contact us via
 MyChart or at 214-645-8898.

References
To learn more about the information in module 5, please visit the following
webpages, which are hosted by the National Cancer Institute and the
American Cancer Society.
Head and Neck Cancer—Patient Version - NCI
Head and Neck Cancers | Cancers of the Head and Neck
ABOUT HEAD & NECK CANCER | Head & Neck Cancer Alliance
https://www.headandneck.org/hnc-resources/
For Patients - American Head & Neck Society

What is a Tracheostomy Tube?
A tracheostomy tube is a medical device
inserted into a small opening in your neck
called a stoma, which leads directly into
your windpipe (trachea).

This tube helps you breathe when you're
unable to breathe normally through your
nose or mouth. It allows air to ﬂow directly
into your lungs and may be used
temporarily or long-term depending on
your condition.

Parts of Your Tracheostomy Tube Continued

The inner cannula is a hollow tube placed in the tracheostomy opening
that remains there during routine use. It's primary purpose is to keep
the airway open and allows it to be cleaned at regular intervals without
removing the tracheostomy tube.

The obturator is a solid insert used during tube insertion or exchange. It
serves as a guide when inserting the tube and is then removed.

Supplies Needed to Clean Your

 Step 1: Wash your hands with soap

Tube Steps Continued
 Step 8: Wet a clean washcloth with clean

 Step 9: Dry your skin with a clean towel.

 Step 10: Wash your hands with soap and
 water.
Suctioning Your Tube

Suctioning
 Your tracheostomy should be suctioned
 if you feel mucus in your chest and are
 unable to cough it out.

 If you are able to cough up the mucus,
 you should not need to suction the
 tracheostomy.

Supplies Needed to Suction Your
 Tracheostomy Tube
1 Suction machine with tubing

2 Sterile suction kit (with red rubber catheter)

3 Clean cup with tap water

4 Normal saline bullets

Suctioning Your Tracheostomy
Tube Steps
 Step 1: Wash your hands.

 Step 2: Turn on the suction machine.

 Step 3: Sit or stand in front of a
 mirror.

 Step 4: Open the suction kit.

 Step 5: Put on the gloves that are
 found inside the kit.

Suctioning Your Tracheostomy Tube Steps Continued
Step 6: Remove the suction catheter from the kit as shown in the
bottom left image, and connect it to the suction line coming from the
machine as shown in the bottom right image. Keep the tip of the
suction catheter as clean as possible.

Suctioning Your Tracheostomy Tube Steps Continued
Step 7: Gently insert the catheter
into your tracheostomy tube
stoma about 8 cm (roughly the
length of your index ﬁnger) or
until you cough.

Step 8: Do not apply suction
when you are pushing the
catheter into your tracheostomy
tube stoma.

Suctioning Your Tracheostomy Tube Steps Continued
Step 9: While slowly pulling the catheter out, pulse the suction by
covering and uncovering the thumbhole of the catheter as shown
below.

Suctioning Your Tracheostomy
Tube Steps Continued
 Step 10: Do not suction more than 10
 seconds.

 Step 11: You can repeat the suction
 again if needed, but ﬁrst take a few
 deep breaths. If suctioning doesn’t
 help, squeeze a saline bullet into
 your tracheostomy tube and repeat
 suction. The saline may cause you to
 cough, but this is normal.

Suctioning Your Tracheostomy
Tube Steps Continued
 Step 12: Rinse the catheter by
 suctioning the water from the cup
 until the catheter and suction
 machine are free of mucous. Remove
 the catheter and throw away the
 catheter and gloves. Never reuse a
 catheter.

 Step 13: Wash your hands with soap
 and water.

Concerning Secretions

 Contact your provider if you notice any of the following:
 ● Yellow-green thick secretions
 ● Pus or foul-smelling discharge
 ● Frank blood or signiﬁcant blood-tinged discharge
 ● Increased volume of secretions that may also be associated
 with fever, cough, or trouble breathing

Changing the Velcro Neck
 Band

Supplies Needed to Change the
 Velcro Neck Band
1 Velcro Neck Band

2 Scissors
2

 It is important to keep a ﬁnger on the
 neck plate at all times to hold the
 tracheostomy tube in place while
 changing ties.

 The velcro band can be changed as
 needed and does not need to be done at
 the same time as suctioning the tube.

Changing the Velcro Neck Band
Steps
Step 1: Wash your hands.

Step 2: Remove the tracheostomy tube
neck band from the package.

Step 3: Separate the long and short end
of the neck band.

Changing the Velcro Neck Band Steps
Step 4: Hold the tracheostomy tube secure and remove one side of the
old ties. Thread the thin velcro tab (of the longer side of the new band)
through the back of the neck plate slit and fold it back to stick it to the
band (as shown below).

Changing the Velcro Neck Band Steps Continued
Step 5: Bring the long end of the cotton band behind your neck.
Remove the second side of the old Velcro band. Thread the thin Velcro
tab of the shorter side of the new band through the back of the other
neck plate slot and fold it back to stick it to the band, as shown below.

Changing the Velcro Neck Band Steps Continued
Step 6: Adjust the neck band to the proper length. You should be able to
ﬁt two ﬁngers under the band, between the band and your neck, as
shown in the bottom right image. Secure it in place by sticking the wide
Velcro tab to the free end of the opposite band. If you have too much
extra band, you can trim the long end of the band with scissors.

Step 7. Discard the old neck band in the trash.

text:
Protecting Your Tracheostomy
Tube and General Comfort Tips

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
Protecting Your Tracheostomy
Tube
Do not let water get into your
tracheostomy tube. This means no
swimming or water sports.

When you take a shower, move the
shower head, so the water hits you
below the tracheostomy tube. When
you rinse your head or neck, cup your
hands over your tracheostomy tube.
You can also wring out a washcloth
and put it over your tracheostomy
tube.

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
Protecting Your Tracheostomy
Tube Continued
 Protect the opening of the
 tracheostomy tube. You can do this
 with a piece of moist gauze, knitted
 tracheostomy cover, or folded
 handkerchief. This is important so
 things like dust, hair, lint, or insects
 cannot get into your tracheostomy
 tube.

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
Improving Comfort for Your
Tracheostomy Tube

 Take in plenty of liquids either by
 mouth or feeding tube once the
 clinical team has deemed it safe.
 This helps keep your mucus
 thinner and easier to cough out.

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
Humidifying the Airway
Humidiﬁcation helps keep your secretions
thin, which reduces the risk of developing
mucus plugs.

Wear your tracheostomy mask (also known as
tracheostomy collar) while sleeping or when
sitting at home for long periods of time.

Use a humidiﬁer with distilled water to
maintain proper airway moisture.

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
Humidifying the Airway Continued
Both tracheostomy masks and HME caps provide
humidiﬁcation of the airway.

A tracheostomy mask or tracheostomy collar
provides external humidiﬁed air or oxygen through
mist.

An HME (heat and moisture exchanger) cap is a small
device attached to the tracheostomy tube that helps
retain heat and moisture during breathing.

Contact provider if you have any additional
questions.

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
Speaking Valves

Tracheostomy speaking valves are
one-way valves, such as the Passy
Muir Valve, which opens when you
breathe in and closes when you
breathe out.

This redirects airﬂow to enable
speech.

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
I Can Manage Cancer



Dental Care
Keep your mouth clean. Brush your teeth and follow up with dentist
regularly for preventative care.

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
Tracheostomy Tube Insertion Difﬁculty Troubleshooting
1) Stay calm and check for signs of trouble breathing.
2) Try to reinsert with the same size tube. May use
 water-based lubricant, but do not force the tube back in.
3) If unsuccessful with the same-size tube, try a tube that is a
 half-size smaller.
4) If a smaller tube fails, insert a endotracheal tube.
5) If a tube is not able to be inserted, call 911 and use a
 bag-valve mask to ventilate.

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
Emergency Situations
 If you have severe problems with
 breathing and suctioning your
 tracheostomy tube does not
 help, call 911 right away. Go to
 the nearest emergency room.

deck: Staying Safe and Comfortable with a Tracheostomy
text:
When to Be Concerned
Come to the hospital right
away if:
 ● Your tracheostomy tube
 comes out, and you are
 unable to put on back in
 yourself
 ● You bleed from your
 tracheostomy stoma or
 notice blood in the tube
 ● You have trouble breathing

Gastrostomy and Nasogastric Tube
Introduction

What is a gastrostomy (G tube)
or nasogastric tube (NG tube)?
 A gastrostomy tube (G tube) and a
 nasogastric tube (NG tube) are types of
 feeding tubes that help provide nutrition,
 ﬂuids, and medications when a person is
 unable to eat or drink enough by mouth.

 They are essential tools for supporting
 health and healing in people with certain
 medical conditions affecting the mouth,
 throat, esophagus, or digestive system.

What is a gastrostomy tube (G tube)?

 A G tube is a soft, ﬂexible tube that
 is placed through the skin of the
 abdomen directly into the stomach.
 It provides a way to deliver nutrition,
 ﬂuids, and medications directly into
 the stomach when oral feeding is
 not possible or safe.

 G tubes are typically used for
 long-term feeding needs (weeks to Source: Cancer Research UK / Wikimedia Commons

 years).

What is a nasogastric tube (NG tube)?

 An NG tube is a thin, ﬂexible tube
 that is inserted through the nose,
 down the throat, and into the
 stomach.

 NG tubes are generally used for
 short-term feeding (days to weeks).

 They may also be used to remove
 stomach contents or administer
 medications. Source: Cancer Research UK / Wikimedia Commons

Parts of the G tube or NG tube

 1. Feeding tube - soft tube inserted into the
 stomach (G tube) or through the nose (NG
 tube)

 2. External Flange/Bumper- Round disk on
 the outside of the body that holds the tube
 in place

 3. Internal Retention Device- Internal
 balloon or bumper that prevents the tube
 from slipping out

Parts of the G tube or NG tube
Continued
4. Extension set- connects to the feeding tube
and allows for feeding or ﬂushing

5. Feeding bag/ syringe- holds liquid nutrition or
medication to be given through the tube

6. Cap or clamp- closes off the tube when not in
use, preventing leakage or air entry

7. Stoma - the small opening on your body’s
surface where a feeding tube (like a G tube or
NG tube) enters and connects to your stomach
or digestive system.
Gastrostomy Tube (G-Tube) Care
After G-tube surgery

Day 1–7 Post-Insertion
 Clean around the tube and stoma (hole
 where the tube goes through the belly
 into the stomach) with mild soap and
 water using gauze or Q-tips.

 Dry thoroughly and place a new piece of
 gauze with a Y cut into the center to
 allow for the gauze to sit around the tube
 and under the external ﬂange.

 Do not use lotions, ointments, or creams
 on the skin. Change the gauze at least
 every 24 hours.

I Can Manage Cancer


After Day 7 Post-Insertion
Remove the gauze and do not replace it. Continue daily cleaning with
mild soap and water around the stoma and tube.

After Day 7 Post-Insertion
Continued
 After cleaning the tube and stoma site,
 rotate or spin the tube in your hand
 several times, this is to make sure it is
 free and can freely spin. If it does not
 rotate or spin, please call the clinic.

 Rotate the tube 360° once daily to
 prevent sticking. Rotate the
 ﬂange/bumper feet at least once a day so
 that the feet do not rest on the same area
 of skin as this can cause damage.

After Day 7 Post-Insertion Continued

 If you still have the stitch on the tube, please call the clinic to schedule an
 appointment to have this removed.

Nutritional Supplement
Information
Before you leave the hospital, you and your
family will be taught how to use your feeding
tube. It’s important to feel comfortable using it
at home.

The tube is used to give you liquid nutrition, but
you can also use it for other liquids like water or
electrolyte drinks.

It is important to administer the nutritional
supplement slowly. Do not to rush the feeding
as it can cause an upset stomach.
G-Tube General Information

Checking Your G Tube Position
Your G tube has a number printed on it near
the plastic disk that rests against your skin
(called the external bumper or ﬂange). This
number shows how far the tube is inserted.
When you ﬁrst got your tube, the doctor or
nurse made a note of this number—it’s your
correct tube position.

Check this number every day.

The number should stay the same unless
your healthcare provider tells you
otherwise.

Checking Your G Tube Position
Continued
 If the number is smaller, the tube may
 have pulled out. Please call the clinic
 immediately.

 If the number is larger, this may cause
 the tube to be too loose. To correct this,
 gently pull the tube up and slide the
 external ﬂange down to the correct
 marking.

G Tube Daily Care
 The external ﬂange/bumper on the G tube
 should rest snugly on top of the skin, but
 there should be enough room for daily
 cleaning underneath.

 After the G tube is inserted, there may be
 a small amount of red or yellowish ﬂuid
 around the new site. This is normal.

G-Tube Daily Care Continued
 Mild leakage around the tube is
 normal. The leakage might be the
 color of the tube feeds,
 stomach/bilious ﬂuid or pinkish.

 Place a new piece of gauze with a Y
 cut into the center to allow for the
 gauze to sit around the tube and
 under the external ﬂange. Change
 this as the gauze gets saturated. DO
 NOT allow saturated gauze to sit on
 your skin for any period of time.

G-Tube Daily Care Continued
 Keep the tube at a 90° angle from the
 skin for the ﬁrst 2 weeks. This will
 help prevent leaking and other
 complications.

 Tuck at least 1 inch of gauze around
 the tube and on top of the bumper,
 and tape the gauze in place. Do not
 tape the tube itself down to the skin.

Chemical Burns
If the skin turns red or is hot, then please
call the clinic and upload a picture of the
site on MyChart. This is usually a chemical
burn from the drainage around the tube, if
this is conﬁrmed, then follow the following
steps:
 -1 Keep the site as dry as possible, even if
 this means replacing the gauze
 frequently.
 -2 Place a thin layer of diaper rash cream
 on the skin around the tube site to
 protect it from drainage.

Showering
You may shower 48 hours after tube
insertion.

You may NOT submerge your tube
site (in a bathtub/swimming
pool/lake/etc.) until at least 2 weeks
after insertion.

It is important to cleanse the site with
mild soapy water and thoroughly dry
the site after it gets wet.

G-Tube Maintenance
 Flush your tube with 30 mL of drinking
 water:
 - Before and after feedings
 - Before and after medications

 Regular ﬂushing will help to prevent the
 tube from clogging. If any feeding or
 medication is left in the tube, this puts
 your tube at a high risk of clogging.

 Some discoloration of the G-tube over
 time is normal.

Replacing Your G-Tube
 Replace your G-tube approximately
 every 6 months, or sooner if
 damaged. Please call the clinic for an
 appointment to replace your tube.

 If the tube cracks or the connections
 come loose sooner, please call the
 clinic for a replacement sooner.

Oral Care
 It is important to maintain good oral care
 even if you may not be eating/drinking
 anything by mouth. This can help prevent
 complications like infection.

 Please gently brush your teeth, gums,
 tongue, and palate at least twice a day if
 you have been told it is safe to do so. You
 should also rinse with mouthwash if it is
 deemed safe (Biotene can help if you are
 experiencing dry mouth).

I Can Manage Cancer



Oral Care
If you are at a high risk of aspiration, you may need to use oral swabs
and a suction catheter.
Troubleshooting Tube Issues

If Your Tube is Clogged
 If you are unable to ﬂush your tube or
 meet signiﬁcant resistance when
 trying to ﬂush, your tube is likely
 clogged. Don’t panic! Here are a few
 things you can try to unclog your
 tube:
 - Make sure your tube is not
 1
 clamped
 - If using a valve at the end of your
 2
 tube, make sure it is in the correct
 position

If Your Tube is Clogged
Continued
 - Carefully massage the tube
 3
 between your thumb and index
 ﬁnger to try to break up any
 clogs. Be careful not to tug or
 pull hard on your tube to keep it
 in place.
 4
 - Hook up an empty syringe and
 slowly and gently try to draw
 back any material that is stuck.

If Your Tube is Clogged Continued
5 Try using warm water to unclog the tube. Use water that is hot but
 not too hot—it should be warm enough to drink comfortably. Gently
 push the warm water into the tube and let it sit for 10 to 15 minutes.
 Then, try ﬂushing the tube again. If you still encounter resistance,
 repeat the process:
 - Add more warm water
 - Gently massage the tube
 - Wait another 10 to 15 minutes

 Keep trying until the tube ﬂushes easily.

If Your Tube is Clogged
Continued
If your tube remains clogged after
attempting the 6 steps described
previously, you should present to the
emergency room to either let medical
professionals attempt to unclog it or have
the tube exchanged.

If Your Tube is Clogged
Continued
Do NOT try to ﬂush your tube with a large
amount of force. This can cause the tubing
to bubble and even burst or leak. If you
notice that your tube is leaking (not from
your skin but from the actual tubing itself)
you will need to have your tube replaced.

Do NOT attempt to insert anything into
your tube to mechanically push the clog
out. This is likely to damage the tube and
is not safe.

Emergency Situations
 If your tube comes out within 4
 weeks of placement, go to the ER
 immediately. The hole can close
 within hours.

 Call the UTSW MDSC Surgery Clinic
 at 214-645-2900 and/or the on-call
 surgeon for instructions.

 This is an emergency. Do not wait
 until morning.
Nasogastric (NG) Tube Care

The Nasogastric (NG) Tube

 ● The NG tube is used to deliver
 nutrients from the nose to the
 stomach.

 ● If the tube is only needed for
 shorter periods of time, the
 NG tube is usually preferred
 over the G tube.


 Source: Cancer Research UK / Wikimedia Commons

How is the NG tube secured?

 ● Often a nasal bridle system is used to
 secure the NG tube. The system has
 small magnets to help keep the tube
 in the nose, which should not be
 painful.
 ● This decreases risk of accidental
 removal including during feedings.
 However, if the bridle is pulled this
 may result in discomfort.

Nutritional Supplement
Information
● Before you leave the hospital, you and your
 family will be taught how to use your
 feeding tube. It’s important to feel
 comfortable using it at home.

● The tube is used to give you liquid nutrition,
 but you can also use it for other liquids like
 water or electrolyte drinks.

● It is important to administer the nutritional
 supplement slowly. Do not to rush the
 feeding as it can cause an upset stomach.

How Tube Feeds Are Delivered

● Bolus feeds: Formula is given manually
 using a syringe several times per day.

● Pump feeds: Formula is delivered slowly
 using a feeding pump (e.g., Kangaroo
 pump), often overnight.

● Your care team will choose the method
 based on your nutritional needs and
 comfort.

NG Tube Clogs
 ● To help keep the tube working
 properly, try to avoid putting
 crushed-up medications or thick
 liquids through the tube, as these
 can cause clogs.

 ● If the tube does get clogged, a
 small amount of carbonated soda
 (like ginger ale or cola) may help
 clear it. If that doesn’t work, you
 may need to visit your doctor’s
 ofﬁce or the emergency room.

Comfort Tips for Nasogastric
(NG) Tube Use
 ● Wearing a nasal feeding tube can
 feel uncomfortable at ﬁrst, and
 it’s common to become very
 aware of its presence.

 ● The tube may occasionally get
 tugged or caught on clothing or
 other objects. While it is unlikely
 to come out, accidental pulling
 can cause discomfort.

Comfort Tips for Nasogastric
(NG) Tube Use
 ● To help manage this discomfort, some
 patients ﬁnd it helpful to secure the
 tube by gently pinning it to the collar
 of their shirt or by looping it up and
 around the ear to keep it out of the
 way.

 ● Finding a method that works for you
 can make daily activities more
 comfortable and help you feel more at
 ease while wearing the tube.

Removing the NG Tube

 ● When it’s time to remove the
 feeding tube, the process is
 quick and can be done during
 a scheduled clinic
 appointment.

 ● Removing the NG tube does
 not require a return to the
 hospital.

Warning signs (to contact your provider)

 ● Bright green output

 ● Bloody drainage

 ● Increased nausea/vomiting

 ● Sudden increase in suction
 output
ADD REFERENCE SLIDE
Management of Incisions

Wound Care for Incisions
Incision: A surgical cut made by the
doctor to access the treatment area,
which is usually closed with stitches or
staples.

Dressings should be changed regularly
to prevent infection of the wound site.

If the dressings are more complex, a
home health nurse may be able to come
to your home to change the dressings.
Talk to your doctor about this option.

How do I avoid irritating the
incision area?

● Wear loose-ﬁtting clothing over the
 donor site.
● Avoid rubbing, soaking, or scrubbing
 the area
● Avoid bathtubs or pools
● Don’t expose it to direct sunlight
 because the skin is extra sensitive

How to prevent infection?
● Wash your hands before touching the
 area.
● Don’t apply creams or ointments unless
 prescribed.
● Watch for signs of infection:
 ○ Increased redness or swelling
 ○ Yellow or green drainage
 ○ Foul smell
 ○ Fever or chills

I Can Manage Cancer


When is pain concerning?
Pain is worrisome if it is continually
increasing over several days.

New or worsening pain at the
incision or donor site is also
worrisome.

When should I be worried about
swelling?
If swelling is gradually worsening over
several consecutive days, this may be a
cause for concern, especially if there is
also redness of the neck or face.

When should I be worried about
drainage?
New or foul smelling drainage is worrisome
especially if you also have fever over
100.4°F (38°C).

Cloudy drainage is is a warning sign as well.
Talk to your surgical team.

I Can Manage Cancer



Saltwater Mouthwash
Saltwater mouth rinses are commonly recommended after many HNC
surgeries to promote oral hygiene, reduce infection risk, and support
healing.

When to use a I Can Manage Cancer




saltwater mouthwash?
 ● Oral Cavity Surgeries:
 ○ Glossectomy (partial or total tongue removal)
 ○ Mandibulectomy
 ○ Maxillectomy
 ○ Oral composite resection
 ○ Mouth cancer surgery
 ● Pharyngectomy
 ● Laryngectomy (total or partial)

These surgeries involve direct incisions in the mouth.
Saltwater rinses help keep wounds clean, reduce bacteria,
and prevent infection without irritating the surgical site.

How to use the mouthwash?
Supplies needed:
● 16 ounce bottle of water
● 1 teaspoon salt
● 1 teaspoon baking soda

1. Keep a bottle by the bathroom and
 kitchen sinks
2. Rinse, gargle, and spit after meals,
 before bed, and anytime your mouth
 feels dry or sore

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
Management of Skin Graft Harvest/
Donor Site

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
What is a donor site?
 You have a skin graft donor site where
 a thin layer of skin was removed (a
 split-thickness skin graft) to help repair
 another area.

 Most commonly, the skin graft is taken
 from the thigh. The donor site may look
 like a rug burn or road rash—this is
 completely normal.

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
Understanding the Donor Site
 Only the outermost layer of skin is
 removed. The full thickness of the skin
 (dermis) is not affected.

 Because the wound is very superﬁcial,
 it generally heals well with minimal
 risk of infection.

 If an infection does occur, it is usually
 very mild.

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
Initial Dressing – Mepilex Ag
 Your donor site has been covered with
 a dressing called Mepilex Ag, which
 contains silver to help prevent infection
 and promote healing.

 This dressing may look bloody or
 crusty over time. This is expected and
 normal.

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
Caring for the Mepilex Ag
Dressing
 Keep the Mepilex Ag dressing in place
 until it falls off on its own. Do not
 remove it unless instructed to do so by
 your doctor.

 If the edges begin to peel up, you may
 trim them carefully with clean scissors

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
What to do if the Mepilex
comes off early?
 If the dressing comes off early or is
 removed, some bleeding may occur.

 Apply gentle pressure to stop any
 bleeding. This is not cause for concern.

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
What to do after the Mepilex comes
off?
Once the Mepilex Ag dressing has naturally fallen
off, begin daily dressing care as follows:
1. There is no speciﬁc need to clean the donor
 area. It is okay to shower and to let water run
 over the site. Do not scrub or soak the area. Pat
 it dry with a clean towel. Do not submerge it in
 a tub or pool.
2. Apply a thin layer of Vaseline or Aquaphor to
 the wound.

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
What to do after the Mepilex comes
off (continued)?
3. Cover the area with a non-adherent dressing, such
as Vaseline gauze, Adaptid, Xeroform, or Telfa.
4. Place a layer of regular gauze over the
non-adherent dressing and tape it down. Do not place
regular gauze directly on the wound, as it may stick
and cause bleeding when removed.
5. Change the dressing once per day, or more often if
it becomes wet or dirty or develops an odor.
6. If the dressing starts to stick to the wound, add
more Vaseline or Aquaphor to keep the area moist.

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
What to expect during healing?
Some bleeding is normal, especially during
dressing changes, because the healing
tissue is very delicate. If bleeding occurs:
● Apply ﬁrm pressure with the dressing
 material for several minutes.
● You may also use gauze ﬂuffs and
 secure them with gentle pressure
 using tape.

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
How do I know the wound is
healed?
The wound is considered healed when a
new layer of skin has formed and there is
no longer any crusting or scabbing.

The new skin is usually pink or purple in
color and may look different or shinier from
the surrounding skin at ﬁrst. This is normal,
and the color will even out over time.

Most donor sites heal within 2-3 weeks

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
How do I care for the new skin
after healing is complete?
Once healed, the new skin is more fragile
and can bleed if scratched or rubbed.

While a dressing is no longer needed, you
may keep it covered with an ACE bandage
or gauze if it is sensitive.

You may apply a non-adherent dressing
with gentle pressure if any minor bleeding
occurs.

deck: Management of Skin Graft Harvest/ Donor Sites
text:
Long-term Skin Care
After new skin has formed, you may begin
applying vitamin E lotion or other
over-the-counter scar cream to help with the
appearance of the scar.
The new skin should be protected from direct
sunlight to reduce the chance of discoloration. This
is especially true during the ﬁrst year.
You may use sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) on the
area once the skin has completely healed. Do not
submerge the area in bathtubs, swimming pools,
lakes, or hot tubs until the new skin has fully
formed.

deck: General Surgical Drains and Drain Management
text:
What is a drain tube?
A drainage tube is left in the surgical
wound at the time of surgery. This tube is
about ¼" thick and is necessary to drain
ﬂuid that accumulates because of
surgery.

Usually, the drain stays in place for a
couple of weeks and patients go home
with this drain.
 drain tube

deck: General Surgical Drains and Drain Management
text:
How do I take care of my drain?
1 The drain needs to be emptied twice daily (or more
 depending on the amount of drainage) and the output needs
 to be recorded.

2 The surgeon will want to know the daily output of the drain
 in milliliters (ML) for each 24-hour period.

3 When the drain output is less than 30-50 ML per 24-hour period, it
 may be ready to be removed.

deck: General Surgical Drains and Drain Management
text:
Will ﬂuid accumulate after
the drain tube is removed?
Occasionally, ﬂuid continues to accumulate
even after the drain is removed.

This can lead to swelling of the skin that
feels soft, like a water balloon.

When you stand up the swelling will drift
down to the lowest portion of the surgical
site.

deck: General Surgical Drains and Drain Management
text:
What should I do if ﬂuid accumulates
after the drain is removed?
1 This ﬂuid (called a seroma) usually needs to be drained but
 the procedure is easy and usually done in the ofﬁce.

2 The skin overlying the area is usually numb from the surgery
 and the ﬂuid can be drained through a small needle inserted
 through the skin.

3 Sometimes this can require several drainage procedures if the
 ﬂuid keeps reaccumulating.

deck: General Surgical Drains and Drain Management
text:
How long can I wait to get the ﬂuid drained?
This is not urgent – you do not need to come in the same day for
this problem.

Waiting even a week or two will be okay
Management of Wound Vacs

What is a wound VAC ?
A Wound VAC (Vacuum-Assisted
Closure) is a medical device that
supports wound healing through
negative pressure therapy.

This increases blood ﬂow in the wound
and helps with healing.

How does it work?
It involves placing a foam dressing
within the wound bed, sealing the area
with an adhesive drape, and connecting
it to a vacuum pump via tubing.

The system gently removes ﬂuid and
debris, reduces swelling, and helps
draw the edges of the wound together.

Why use a wound VAC?
Wound VACs are commonly used after major
head and neck cancer surgeries, especially
when there are large or complex surgical
wounds, tissue ﬂaps, or areas at high risk for
ﬂuid collection.
They help the area heal by removing ﬂuid,
improving blood ﬂow, preventing infection,
and protecting tissue ﬂaps.

What to expect?
The VAC device will remain in place
continuously, typically connected to portable
suction.
The dressing is sealed tightly to the skin, and
you may feel a light pulling or suction
sensation. Mild discomfort can occur but should
not be severe.
The dressing is usually changed every 2–3 days
by trained providers, either in the hospital or
clinic setting.

Daily management of the
Wound VAC
Avoid disconnecting or turning off the
Wound VAC unless instructed. Keep the
tubing free of kinks and below the wound
site to allow proper drainage.

When to Call Your Care
Team

Make sure the seal is intact—if you hear air
leaks or see dressing lifting, notify your care
team. If the canister becomes full or alarms
sound, contact your provider or home health
nurse.

Hygiene and activity
precautions
● Do not shower while the VAC is in place
 unless your provider has approved a
 special cover or dressing.
● Avoid submerging the VAC or dressing in
 water.
● Be cautious with neck movement and
 avoid pulling on the tubing.
● Limit strenuous activities and avoid laying
 directly on the VAC dressing site to
 prevent pressure disruption.
Lymphedema

I Can Manage Cancer



What is cancer-related Lymphedema
● Lymphedema refers to swelling caused by the buildup of lymph ﬂuid beneath the
 skin. The lymphatic system normally functions to collect and transport excess ﬂuid,
 proteins, and waste products from body tissues back into the bloodstream. It also
 plays a key role in ﬁltering out bacteria, viruses, and other harmful substances.
● When lymph nodes or vessels are damaged or obstructed, lymph ﬂuid cannot drain
 effectively. This results in ﬂuid accumulation and swelling.

What are the causes?
 Cancer related lymphedema occurs when
 the lymphatic system is blocked or
 damaged from the effects of cancer cancer
 treatments.

 Common causes:
 ● Surgery to remove lymph nodes
 ● Radiation treatment for cancer
 ● Tumor growth from cancer

What increases the risk?

 The following factors may make you more
 likely to develop this complication:

 ● Older age
 ● Obesity
 ● Rheumatoid or inﬂammatory arthritis
 ● History of lymphedema

What are the physical exam
signs of lymphedema?
 ● Sensation of heaviness, tightness, or
 fullness in the affected area
 ● Mild swelling that may come and go,
 especially at the end of the day
 ● Clothing, jewelry, or compression
 garments feeling tighter than usual
 ● Skin changes, such as slight pufﬁness,
 decreased elasticity, or indentation when
 pressed
 ● Aching, tingling, or discomfort in the
 limb or region
 ● Reduced range of motion in the neck,
 shoulder, or affected limb

How to treat lymphedema?
 Compression Garments
 ● Sleeves or stockings to maintain pressure
 ● Elevated the limb above the level of your heart if
 possible
 Compression Bandaging
 ● Multi-layer wraps to reduce swelling
 Pneumatic Compression Pump
 ● External pump with inﬂatable sleeve to promote
 drainage
 Surgery (for severe cases)
 ● Reserved for chronic, refractory lymphedema
 Complete Decongestive Therapy (CDT)
 ● Manual lymphatic drainage (specialized massage)
 ● Compression therapy
 ● Gentle exercise
 ● Skin care

Dysphagia Strategies and

What is Dysphagia?

● Dysphagia, or difﬁculty swallowing, is a common
 postoperative symptom.
● Postoperative dysphagia can result from swelling,
 nerve irritation, muscle weakness, or structural
 changes that disrupt the normal swallowing
 mechanism.

Speech Therapy
 ● Speech therapy plays an integral role in your
 ability to swallow and is essential to optimize
 your health while undergoing treatment
 ● A wide range of conditions, illnesses, and their
 treatments can disrupt the process of
 swallowing which can lead to choking,
 malnutrition, and other problems
 ● UTSW Speech Therapy department will
 provide you more strategies to successfully
 navigate your nutritional status before and
 after surgery.

Exercise #1: Jaw Resistance

1. Slightly open your mouth and press chin
 against the palm
2. Let your elbow be on your knee
3. Feel the engagement in the center neck
 and below the chin
4. Sustain the position for 10 seconds
5. Keep breathing (5 repetitions, 3-5 times
 a day)

Exercise #2: Tongue Hold
(Masako)
1. Hold your tongue between your teeth
2. Swallow while keeping your tongue
 between your teeth
This exercise strengthens the muscles in the
back of your throat.
(5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)

Exercise #3: Effortful
Swallow
1. Swallow with extra force
2. Feel your tongue against the roof of your
 mouth as you swallow
 (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)

Exercise #4: Tongue
Pull-back
1. Say the “k-k-k-k-k” harshly
2. Feel the engagement of the back of the
 tongue
 (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)

Exercise #5: Pharyngeal
Constriction
1. Say a high pitched “ee” sound for 5
 seconds
2. Watch yourself in the mirror and make
 sure your neck muscles are engaged
 (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)

Exercise #6: Mendelsohn
Maneuver
1. Feel the top of your larynx (Adam’s
 apple) moving upward during a swallow
2. At the highest point of your swallow
 (when you hear the clicking sound), try to
 hold the larynx up.
3. Hold your breath for 5 seconds.
This exercise helps lift your larynx and opens
the top of your food pipe (esophagus). This
can help clear out any leftover food stuck in
your throat. (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)

When are these exercises useful?
 Helpful for:

 ● Laryngectomy (partial or total)
 ● Oropharynx surgery
 ● Radiation to throat or neck

 Beneﬁts:

 ● Keeps swallowing muscles strong
 ● Speeds up recovery after treatment
 ● Lowers risk of feeding tube or
 aspiration
 ● Helps you keep eating by mouth
 longer

Spinal Accessory Nerve
 Exercises

What is the spinal accessory
nerve?
The spinal accessory nerve is located in
the back of your upper shoulder. When
the nerve is injured, it can cause pain and
can greatly reduce the range of motion in
that shoulder

Exercise #1: Shoulder
Shrugs
1. Shoulder shrugs can strengthen the injured
 area.
2. Stand with your legs hip-distance apart.
3. Shrug your shoulders up and lower them
 down as far as you comfortably can
4. Do a total of 10 repetitions
5. As you progress hold weights in your
 hands as you do this exercise

Exercise #2: Supine
Shoulder Rotation
1. Use a bed or mat for another
 strengthening exercise
2. Lie on your back and bend your elbows
3. Your upper arm should be at your side
 horizontal to the ground and your lower
 arms in the air perpendicular to the
 ground
4. Slowly bring your hands down to the mat
 or bed and back up in the air
5. Do a total of 10 repetitions

Exercise #3: Shoulder
Elevation with Wand
1. The American Physical Therapy Association
 suggests this exercise that involves using a
 cane, broomstick or dowel
2. Lie on your back holding the cane, broomstick or
 dowel with your hands resting on your upper
 legs
3. Your hands should be about 18 inches apart, and
 your palms should be facing up
4. Slowly lift your arms as far over your head as is
 comfortable, leading with the uninjured arm
5. Hold for 5 seconds and return to your original
 position do a total of ﬁve repetitions

Exercise #4: Wall Slide
1. The APTA also recommends a standing
 exercise to rehabilitate a spinal accessory
 nerve injury
2. Stand close to a wall, facing sideways
3. Slide your injured arm up the wall using
 your ﬁngers to walk up the wall, palms
 facing down
4. Keep sliding your hand until you feel a
 stretch and hold the position for 5 seconds
5. Slowly drop your arm and do a total of ﬁve
 repetitions
6. Do not make the mistake of turning your
 body towards the wall

Exercise #5: Wall Press
1. Stand facing a wall for this
 strengthening exercise
2. You should be two to three feet away
 from the wall
3. Put your hands on the wall at
 shoulder level and press against it
4. As you do this, squeeze your shoulder
 blades together and then separate
 them
5. Return to your starting position
6. Do a total of 10 repetitions

When are these exercises useful?
 Helpful for: Neck dissection surgery
 (especially levels II–V)

 Beneﬁts:

 ● Protects shoulder and neck
 strength
 ● Reduces risk of shoulder pain and
 stiffness
 ● Improves posture and range of
 motion
 ● Easier return to normal activity after
 surgery

General Reasons for
Postoperative Radiation

Why do I need radiation after
surgery?
You may need radiation after surgery based on
certain risk features found in your tumor.
Radiation is used to reduce the risk of cancer
returning after surgery.

When cancer comes back after treatment, it's
called a recurrence. Radiation helps lower the
chances of this happening.

Common Reasons for
Postoperative Radiation
● Advanced stage primary tumor: If your
 tumor is classiﬁed as T3 or T4 (larger or
 more invasive tumors), radiation is typically
 recommended.
● Perineural invasion: If cancer is found
 spreading along small nerves, this
 increases the risk of recurrence.
● Lymphovascular invasion: Cancer cells
 found in small blood vessels or lymphatic
 vessels suggest a higher likelihood of
 spread.

Common Reasons for
Postoperative Radiation (cont.)
● Close margins: If the tumor is close to the
 edge of the surgical specimen, there may
 be microscopic cancer left behind.
● Lymph node involvement:
 ○ Multiple lymph nodes with cancer
 (pathologic N2 or N3 disease)
 ○ Large lymph nodes involved
 ○ Involvement of low or posterior neck
 lymph nodes (levels 4 or 5)

Postoperative Radiation and
 Chemotherapy

What is chemotherapy?

Chemotherapy is medicine that travels
through your whole body to kill cancer cells.
It’s usually given by IV or as a pill, and it
works by targeting fast-growing cells like
cancer.

Why do I need both radiation
and chemotherapy after surgery?
In some cases, chemotherapy is added to
radiation therapy to improve treatment
outcomes. This decision is based on certain
high-risk features found during surgery.

This combination of treatments may increase
side effects but can improve the chances of
cure in high-risk patients.

Common Reasons for
Postoperative Radiation with
Chemotherapy
● Positive surgical margins: If cancer cells are
 seen right at the edge of the removed tissue,
 this indicates that not all cancer may have
 been removed.
● Extracapsular spread (ECS): If cancer has
 spread outside a lymph node into
 surrounding tissue, chemotherapy is typically
 recommended in addition to radiation.

Timing of Postoperative
 Radiation

When do I start receiving
postoperative radiation therapy?
Radiation is most effective when started
soon after surgery, once you have healed but
before too much time passes.

What is a typical timeline?

● Start radiation within 6 weeks of
 surgery, ideally.
● This allows enough time for surgical
 healing while ensuring radiation is still
 effective.
● Delays beyond 8 weeks may reduce
 treatment success, so it's important to
 keep appointments and complete
 pre-radiation evaluations on time.

Visiting the Dentist

Why do I need to see
the dentist?
Radiation to the head and neck can
damage your salivary glands and
cause xerostomia (dry mouth)
which increases the risk of:
 ● Cavities and dental infections
 ● Osteoradionecrosis (jawbone
 damage)
 ● Other long-term dental
 complications

What do I need to do?

● Schedule a pre-radiation dental
 evaluation at least a few weeks
 before starting radiation.
● Your dentist will check for and
 treat any dental issues
 beforehand.
● You may need extractions, ﬁllings,
 or cleanings to reduce the risk of
 problems during or after
 treatment.

Goals of Pre-Radiation
Oral/Dental Evaluation:
● Patient education (both oral and
 written) about dental risks and
 preventive care
● Complete head and neck dental
 exam, including x-rays
● Identify and treat sources of
 infection before radiation
Maintaining Dental Health

Dry Mouth Management
● Increase hydration
● Avoid caffeine and alcohol
● Use salivary stimulants (e.g.,
 xylitol gum/lozenges, sorbitol,
 pilocarpine, cevimeline)
● Use alcohol-free mouthwash
 (e.g., 0.1% chlorine dioxide rinse)
● Use salivary substitutes (e.g.,
 gels with lysozyme, lactoferrin,
 calcium phosphate)

Dental Caries Prevention
● Brush and ﬂoss daily
● Use ﬂuoride treatments:
 ○ 1.1% NaF gel or dentifrice
 daily
 ○ Fluoride varnish 3x/year
 ○ Calcium phosphate
 rinses/gels
● Frequent dental checkups

Fungal Infection Prevention
● Antifungal lozenges or rinses
● Systemic antifungals if needed (consult infectious disease
 specialist)

Extractions and Jaw Tightness
● Determine if tooth extractions are needed before RT (at least 2
 weeks prior)
● Coordinate any future extractions with your oncology team
● Monitor and manage trismus (jaw tightness)

Post-Treatment Dental
Management
● Continue managing dry mouth
 and trismus
● Maintain strict oral hygiene and
 caries prevention
● Prevent/manage
 osteoradionecrosis
● Avoid implants or extractions
 without radiation oncologist
 consultation
● Dental visits every 6 months or
 more frequently if xerostomia or
 new dental issues arise
